Section  11,  read with section  11B,  of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 -  Powers and functions of board  - Whether a listed entity operating in Indian securities market cannot rely upon private confidentiality arrangements or foreign data protection provisions to defeat or dilute its statutory disclosure obligations under Indian securities laws - Held, yes - Whether where a listed entity chooses to structure its operations through overseas subsidiaries and thereafter consolidates financial results of such entities into its public disclosures, it remains under a continuing obligation to maintain and furnish sufficient underlying information to enable regulatory verification and investor transparency - Held, yes - Whether where REL’s consolidated financial performance was almost entirely dependent on its overseas subsidiaries, particularly Valcambi SA, but company had systematically withheld financial statements of these entities from public domain and had failed to provide necessary underlying data (party-wise details of vendors, customers, etc.) to Investigating Authority despite repeated summons, REL had obstructed investigation and impaired SEBI’s ability to verify authenticity of consolidated financial statements, thereby violating Section 11(2)(ia) and 11C(3) - Held, yes - Whether where REL had furnished contradictory figures at different stages of investigation, REL had impeded SEBI’s ability to independently verify reported sales figures and furnishing of inconsistent and misleading information by REL had obstructed and hampered investigative process and demonstrated non-cooperation with Investigating Authority - Held, yes - Whether thus, REL had, prima facie, violated Section 11(2)(ia) - Held, yes [Paras 22, 23, 27, 65 and 231]

Section 115JB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Minimum alternate tax (Computation of book profit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - As on 31st March 2016, assessee had outstanding Zero Coupon Unsecured Optionally Fully Convertible Debentures (ZOFCDS) amounting to Rs. 15,544.57 Crores and Zero Coupon Unsecured Fully Convertible Debentures (FCDs) of Rs. 279.90 crores totalling to Rs. 15,824.47 crores issued to RIL, its holding company - Said Convertible Debentures, were disclosed as "long-term borrowings" in audited financial statements as on 31-3-2016 as per requirements of Indian GAAP - Since 'Ind AS' had become applicable to assessee-company with effect from financial year 2016-17, it made a transition to Ind AS - Accordingly, it prepared and presented its financial statements from financial year ending 31" March 2017 under Ind AS and re-classified Convertible Debentures as equity instrument in its first Ind AS balance sheet and presented them as "Instruments entirely Equity in nature" - CIT, in order passed under section 263, held that all financial instruments under consideration were Compound Financial Instruments (CFI) and, therefore, amount represented by said instruments was taxable as book profit under secton 115JB(2C) - Whether for categorizing a financial instruments as CFI, there was to be a liability component embedded in it - Held, yes - Whether there are two situations in relation to financial instrument which can be reckoned as financial liability; firstly, there is a contractual obligation to make settlement either by monetary payment or by delivering any other financial asset; or secondly, settlement has to be made by exchange of variable number of its own equity instruments - Held, yes - Whether since settlement of convertible debentures issued by assessee would be through exchange of own equity instruments of assessee-company only and not by any financial liability as defined in Ind AS 32 and this exchange, as per terms, would be of a fixed number of equity shares, criteria to classify financial instrument of convertible debentures were not indicative of any Compounding Financial Instrument albeit it was equity - Held, yes - Whether since aforesaid convertible debentures were purely in nature of equity and there was no kind of financial liability or any interest component, which could be ascertained or determined on said debentures, there would be no transition amount requiring any adjustment in book profit as per section 115JB(2C) - Held, yes [Para 85] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where settlement of convertible debentures issued by assessee would be through exchange of its own equity instruments and not by any financial liability as defined in Ind AS 32 and this exchange, as per terms, would be of a fixed number of equity shares, criteria to classify financial instrument of convertible debentures were not indicative of any compounding financial instrument albeit it was equity; therefore, there would not be any transition amount requiring any adjustment in book profit as per section 115JB(2C)

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Company - Assessable as - When Assessing Officer in income-tax proceedings is to lift corporate veil, he should first come to conclusion that entities-in- question were created for purpose of avoiding tax; where investment companies-in-question of an industrial group, namely, FIPL and HIPL were functioning as separate legal entities in their own name and out their objects in terms of their memorandum of association and it was found that transactions between those investment companies and their holding company were at arm's length, finding of Assessing Officer that those entitles were mere paper entities or dummy entities was not justified

Section  47,  read with sections  2(47)  and  56, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  70,  read with sections  2(109)  and  92, of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Capital gains  -  Transactions not regarded as transfer  (Shares) - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessee, a French based company, was holding 60 per cent of shares in an Indian company (VSIPL) since 2012 - Assessee acquired remaining 40 per cent stake from its JV partner in 2018 after joint venture failed - In December 2019, it sold 100 per cent of VSIPL shares to another wholly owned Indian subsidiary, VIPL, claiming exemption under section 47(iv) - Subsequently, VSIPL merged with VIPL under fast-track merger process - Assessing Officer opined that transaction was in nature of trade and not a capital asset as assessee had acquired assets only in year 2018 to sell it in 2019 - He, thus, treated entire consideration as income from other sources - It was noted that assessee had held major portion of shares in VSIPL as investments since 2012 and only acquired remaining 40 per cent in 2018 - It was also noted that assessee held 100 per cent shares in VSIPL and VIPL and both these companies were Indian companies - Whether transaction resulted in a reorganization of shareholding without any change in ultimate beneficial ownership, thereby indicating continuity of economic interest where capital asset continued to exist in India - Held, yes - Whether since there was no material to suggest that transaction was circular, self-cancelling, or devoid of real economic effect, transaction could not be disregarded merely on basis of perceived tax advantage - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned transaction was a bona fide transfer squarely covered by section 47(iv) and addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section 115JB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Minimum alternate tax (Computation of book profit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - As on 31st March 2016, assessee had outstanding Zero Coupon Unsecured Optionally Fully Convertible Debentures (ZOFCDS) amounting to Rs. 15,544.57 Crores and Zero Coupon Unsecured Fully Convertible Debentures (FCDs) of Rs. 279.90 crores totalling to Rs. 15,824.47 crores issued to RIL, its holding company - Said Convertible Debentures, were disclosed as "long-term borrowings" in audited financial statements as on 31-3-2016 as per requirements of Indian GAAP - Since 'Ind AS' had become applicable to assessee-company with effect from financial year 2016-17, it made a transition to Ind AS - Accordingly, it prepared and presented its financial statements from financial year ending 31" March 2017 under Ind AS and re-classified Convertible Debentures as equity instrument in its first Ind AS balance sheet and presented them as "Instruments entirely Equity in nature" - CIT, in order passed under section 263, held that all financial instruments under consideration were Compound Financial Instruments (CFI) and, therefore, amount represented by said instruments was taxable as book profit under secton 115JB(2C) - Whether for categorizing a financial instruments as CFI, there was to be a liability component embedded in it - Held, yes - Whether there are two situations in relation to financial instrument which can be reckoned as financial liability; firstly, there is a contractual obligation to make settlement either by monetary payment or by delivering any other financial asset; or secondly, settlement has to be made by exchange of variable number of its own equity instruments - Held, yes - Whether since settlement of convertible debentures issued by assessee would be through exchange of own equity instruments of assessee-company only and not by any financial liability as defined in Ind AS 32 and this exchange, as per terms, would be of a fixed number of equity shares, criteria to classify financial instrument of convertible debentures were not indicative of any Compounding Financial Instrument albeit it was equity - Held, yes - Whether since aforesaid convertible debentures were purely in nature of equity and there was no kind of financial liability or any interest component, which could be ascertained or determined on said debentures, there would be no transition amount requiring any adjustment in book profit as per section 115JB(2C) - Held, yes [Para 85] [In favour of assessee]

Section  56  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income from other sources  -  Chargeable as(Gifts) - Assessment year  2021-22  - Assessee company engaged in business of beauty wellness and hospitality services, issued shares as per two valuation reports - As per first valuation certificate, fair market value was Rs. 50,176 and in second valuation certificate, fair market value per share was Rs. 1.61 lakhs - Assessing Officer found justification filed by assessee for increase in valuation of shares within period of 8 months to be unsatisfactory and made addition under section 56(2)(viib) and section 56(2)(x) - Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition observing that assessee being a venture capital undertaking and investments being by a SEBI-registered Alternate Investment Fund were exempt from rigours of section 56(2)(viib) - Revenue contended that investment by Wipro Enterprises Ltd. (WEL) was not covered, as WEL was neither a venture capital undertaking nor a SEBI-registered fund - Whether since WEL was admittedly not a SEBI-registered Alternate Investment Fund, very basis of giving relief to assessee by Commissioner (Appeals) was incorrect - Held, yes - Whether however, since assessee had furnished various other details of WEL in support of its contention that source of investment was duly explained along with relevant documentary evidences and shares had been issued at fair market value arrived at by registered valuer applying discounted cash flow method, issue deserved to be restored back to file of Commissioner (Appeals) for afresh adjudication - Held, yes [Paras 8 & 9] [Matter remanded]

Section  9,  read with section  90,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and  article 13    of DTAA between India and Netherlands - Income – Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Capital gains - Buy-back of shares) - Assessment year  2009-10  - Assessee, a Netherlands resident, held 99.98 per cent of shares in an Indian company, HIIPL - During relevant year, HIIPL offered a buy-back under which assessee sold 2.14 crore equity shares (about 24 per cent) at Rs. 23.10 per share for about Rs. 49.43 crores - Assessee initially offered long-term capital gains of about Rs. 6.17 crores to tax in its return - TPO determined ALP at Rs. 80.77 per share and proposed an upward adjustment of about Rs. 123.41 crores by adopting sale consideration at about Rs. 172.85 crores instead of Rs. 49.43 crores - Assessee raised an additional ground that buy-back was not taxable in India under article 13(5) of India–Netherlands DTAA on ground that gains were realised in course of a ‘corporate organisation, reorganisation, amalgamation, division or similar transaction’ and were taxable only in Netherlands - Whether since transaction of buy-back of shares by HIIPL from assessee, being transfer of shares within same corporate group, constituted a corporate reorganisation, capital gains arising to assessee from such buy-back were taxable only in Netherlands and not in India under article 13(5) - Held, yes (per majority view) [Paras 21, 28 and 29] [In favour of assessee]

I.Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustments - Interest) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee made certain trade advances to AEs and submitted that since amounts advanced to AE partook character of equity, no interest was chargeable thereon - TPO however adopted 14 per cent as appropriate bench mark price and made adjustment towards interest on advance provided to AEs - Assessee admitted that since in subsequent assessment year, Tribunal had held adjustments at LIBOR + 2 per cent/EURIBOR + 2 per cent, he would have no objection if same rates were adopted - Whether in view of orders of DRP and Tribunal in other assessment years in assessee's own case, Assessing Officer/TPO was to be directed to adopt EURIBOR + 2 per cent rate of interest for making adjustment under provisions - Held, yes [Para 5.1] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Where assessee made trade advances to AEs, interest was chargeable and TPO was to be directed to adopt EURIBOR + 2 per cent rate of interest as appropriate bench mark price and make adjustments towards interest and advance provided to AEs  IT/ILT: Investments in nature of equity, cannot be treated as loans and advances and hence, no adjustment was warranted on share application money pending allotment  IT/ILT: Transaction of providing corporate guarantee involves service rendered to AE and, therefore, provisions of transfer pricing can be invoked in respect of such a transaction  IT/ILT: Income from settlement of patent infringement credited to profit and loss account falls under category of 'other income' and not operating revenue  IT/ILT: Foreign exchange fluctuation gain/loss are part of operating profits of assessee as well as comparable companies while undertaking ALP adjustments  IT/ILT: Where TPO rejected comparables selected by assessee on grounds of use of multiple year data, inappropriate filters, etc., but DRP did not adjudicate objections raised by assessee, selection of comparables was to be restored back to authorities for re-examination  IT/ILT: Taxability or otherwise of amount in hands of JV of assessee would not determine basis of taxation in case of assessee

Section 69, read with sections 69A and 80-1 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments - Block assessment period 1987-88 to 1995-96 -Assessees were five HUFs and seven companies belonging to 'V’ group -Group companies were direct control and management of 'V’ brothers, kartas of respective HUFs, who had total control over Board of Management as well as general body meeting of shareholders - Pursuant to search operations under section 132, substantial agricultural income was shown by assessee-HUF by way of cash deposits in bank accounts was admittedly not genuine - Such deposits made on day-to-day basis were later withdrawn for investments in seven companies as well as for advancing loans to family members- Assessing Officer treated inflation of agricultural income as undisclosed income and made additions on substantive basis in block assessments of HUFs while making protective additions in respect of seven companies - Whether since no evidence whatsoever with regard to agricultural activities carried out by assessees as well as details of sale bill of agricultural products and particulars of agricultural expenses had been produced, estimate of agricultural income of entire 'V’ family during block period made by Assessing Officer was to be upheld along with addition on account of inflation - Held, yes - Whether cash deposits in banks of HUFs to extent of inflation of agricultural income having remained unexplained, were liable to be treated as undisclosed income under section 69 - Held, yes - Whether income had to be assessed substantively in hands of HUFs in light of realities and actualities of situation whereunder assessee-HUFs had received income by utilizing instrumentality of corporate entity as mere puppets - Held, yes - Whether when corporate veil was lifted, very applicability of section 88 of Indian Trusts Act, 1882 became redundant and gains arising to directors under such circumstances would 
not be governed by said provision - Held, yes - Whether for 
above reasons, substantive additions made in cases of HUFs were 
to be sustained whereas corresponding protective additions in 
cases of group companies were to be deleted - Held, yes

Section 41, read with section 111, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Member - Petitioner, a non-resident Indian entrepreneur in information technology business, remitted funds in India to ‘SN’ for incorporation and promotion of respondent-company - ‘SN’ incorporated company and also allotted 2000 shares of Rs. 100 each at a premium of Rs. 10,782.70 per share to petitioner - Petitioner alleged that allotment of said shares was without his knowledge and consent and filed a petition under section 111 for rectification in Register of Members of company by cancelling allotment of impugned shares - Whether though correspondences between petitioner, ‘SN’ and petitioner’s brother during relevant period spoke of investment pattern and business of company, yet they did not make any reference to purported allotment in favour of petitioner - Held, yes - Whether impugned shares were allotted in favour of petitioner at board meeting held on 26-11-2001 but same was in variance with stand taken by company that shares were allotted to petitioner on 22-11-2001 - Held, yes - Whether though certificate of chartered accountant of company showed that premium was arrived at by mutual agreement between company and petitioner, yet there was no record either to substantiate any such mutual agreement between parties or due compliance with guidelines issued by erstwhile Controller of Capital Issues in valuation of impugned shares - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, allotment of impugned shares in favour of petitioner was irregular and not in consonance with Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer of Issue of Security by a Person Resident Outside India) Regulations, 2000, which would be a sufficient cause to order rectification in Register of Members of company - Held, yes

Section 9, read with section 139, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section 9, read with section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, read with section 9 of the Companies Act, 2013 and article 6  of the OECD Model Convention – Income – Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Income From Immovable Property - Scope of Provision) - Assessment years 2011-12 to 2017-18 – Respondents, husband and wife, residents of India, held shares in a company (CCL) incorporated in the British Virgin Islands, which owned properties in United Kingdom – Said company earned rental income and generated capital gains on sale of properties and paid applicable taxes in United Kingdom – Assessing Officer held that respondents were real and beneficial owners of assets of company and treated income of company as income of respondents by invoking doctrine of substance over form and lifting corporate veil – It was noted that company was registered in British Virgin Islands and properties were situated in United Kingdom; shares in company were acquired through banking channels under permitted Liberalised Remittance Scheme of RBI; company had also obtained loans from banks in United Kingdom for purchase of properties; company earned rental income and generated gains on sale of properties in its own right and paid taxes thereon – Whether respondents, being shareholders of company, even if holding entire shareholding, were only owners of shares of company and not owners of properties as such – Held, yes – Whether income earned by company could, by no stretch of imagination, be treated to be income of its shareholders – Held, yes – Whether only dividend income, if and when received by shareholders, could be subjected to tax and not income of company itself – Held, yes – Whether there is no provision under Income-tax Act, 1961 under which such income of company can be taxed in hands of shareholders merely because they are residents of India – Held, yes – Whether action of Assessing Officer in invoking doctrine of substance over form and lifting corporate veil to tax income of company in hands of respondents was not backed by statutory framework and was thus, unsustainable – Held, yes [Paras 24 to 27] [In favour of assessee]INTERNATIONAL TAXATION: Where Indian residents held shares in a foreign company incorporated in British Virgin Islands which owned properties in UK, rental income and capital gains earned and taxed abroad by company could not be assessed in hands of shareholders in India by treating them as beneficial owners or by lifting corporate veil, since only dividend income, if any, received by shareholders is taxable in India and there is no provision under Act to tax company’s income in shareholders’ hands merely on account of residency or investment

I. Section 9  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with article 23 of DTAA between India and France - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Method of Elimination of double taxation) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee, a French company, was engaged in business of providing various support, sustenance and developmental service to its Group companies across world - Assessee had given a corporate guarantee to BNP Paribas, a French Bank on behalf of its various subsidiaries worldwide - Two Indian subsidiaries of assessee were sanctioned credit facilities by Indian Branches of BNP Paribas, which credit facilities were secured by said corporate guarantee given by assessee - Assessee had charged guarantee commission at for said corporate guarantees - Assessing Officer had taxed same by holding it to be 'Other income' under article 23 - Whether income clearly arose in France because guarantee had been given by a French company to a French Bank, in France and, therefore, article 23 had no application as income did not arise in India - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, guarantee commission received by assessee could not held to be taxable in India - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of revenue]IT/ILT : Where assessee, a French company, had given corporate guarantee to French bank, on behalf of its Indian subsidiaries which were extended credit facilities by branch of said bank, guarantee commission received by assessee company did not accrue in India, income clearly arose in France because guarantee had been given by assessee, a French Bank, in France and, therefore, article 23 had no applicability  IT/ILT : Provisions of article 13 of Indo-French DTAA prescribing a cap of 10% on rate of tax, read with article 2 thereof, would prevail over provisions of domestic income-tax and thus tax liability on royalty income shall be capped at 10% and rate of tax @ 10% cannot be enhanced by including surcharge and education cess separately

Section  56 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with rule  11UA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 -  Income from other sources -  Chargeable as (Share premium) - Assessment year  2016-17 - Assessee-company, engaged in business of providing software support/maintenance services, held 20 per cent equity stake in SAFL, a company engaged in FM radio business - SAFL required to raise funds for investing in its business and had accordingly offered rights issue at a price of ?20 per share including share premium of ?10 - Assessee subscribed to 2.63 crore shares of SAFL at an aggregate value of ?52.60 crore - Assessee required to raise funds for subscribing to rights issue offered by SAFL and thus in turn it offered rights issue to its shareholders - For purpose of determining FMV, assessee engaged an expert who furnished valuation report determining FMV of shares of assessee at ?2771.65 per share - Assessing Officer rejected FMV of shares determined by assessee by DCF method and proceeded to determine FMV of shares issued by assessee at its book value and concluded that same was in negative - Thus, Assessing Officer added a sum of ?30.37 crore as assessee's income from other sources under section 56(2)(viib) - It was noted that shares issued by assessee to its shareholders were to fund purchase of shares of SAFL - Value at which SAFL's shares were subscribed by assessee had not been objected to by revenue in assessment of SAFL - In any event same was substantiated by an expert report who had valued shares of SAFL by DCF method - Whether expert report could not be rejected on ground of general disclaimers without Assessing Officer pointing out any material error in data as used by expert - Held, yes - Whether since DCF method was one of methods that could be adopted by assessee under rule 11UA(2)(b) for determining FMV of unquoted equity shares, assessee's valuation of FMV was to be accepted - Held, yes [Paras 18 and 19] [In favour of assessee]

company earned rental income and generated gains on sale of properties in its own right and paid taxes thereon – Whether respondents, being shareholders of company, even if holding entire shareholding, were only owners of shares of company and not owners of properties as such – Held, yes – Whether income earned by company could, by no stretch of imagination, be treated to be income of its shareholders – Held, yes – Whether only dividend income, if and when received by shareholders, could be subjected to tax and not income of company itself – Held, yes – Whether there is no provision under Income-tax Act, 1961 under which such income of company can be taxed in hands of shareholders merely because they are residents of India – Held, yes – Whether action of Assessing Officer in invoking doctrine of substance over form and lifting corporate veil to tax income of company in hands of respondents was not backed by statutory framework and was thus, unsustainable – Held, yes [Paras 24 to 27] [In favour of assessee]

Regulation 10 of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 1997 - Acquisition of fifteen per cent or more of shares or voting rights of any company B Ltd. was a company incorporated in England while UBL was a company incorporated in Mauritius whose entire issued share capital was acquired by UIC - UBL held 26.01 per cent shares of target company, incorporated in India - Under a share purchase agreement entered into between UIC and ‘B’ Ltd. in England on 14-2-2005, B Ltd. acquired entire equity share capital of UBL and, thus, also acquired indirectly equity shares of target company and made a public announcement to that effect on 15-2-2005 - Soon after public announcement, appellant, holding 8.5 per cent shares in target company, filed complaint that target company had entered into shareholder agreement, to which UBL, appellant through its predecessor and other financial institutions which were shareholders, were party, which contained a provision for pre-emption if any of parties to agreement desired to sell off their shares and, thus, it had a right of pre-emption before B Ltd. could acquire/purchase shares of UBL - SEBI made B Ltd. to modify draft letter of public announcement so as to disclose to shareholders disputes pending in different fora and dismissed appellant’s complaint holding that there was no violation of Regulations - Whether since dispute regarding pre-emption right of shareholders of target company was pending in civil court and some arbitration proceedings were also pending in England, SEBI could not intervene in matter and, therefore, rightly dismissed complaint - Held, yes - Whether further agreement between B Ltd. and UIC being an agreement between two foreign companies whereby shares of another foreign company were acquired outside India, validity of such an agreement could be challenged only according to laws of domicile of those companies and, therefore, there being no merit in appeal, same was to be dismissed - Held, yes

IV. Section 90 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 26 of the DTAA between India and France - Double taxation relief - Where agreement exists [Non-discrimination] - Assessment years 2002-03 and 2003-04 - Whether business income of non-resident company is taxable at rate applicable to foreign company and not rate of tax applicable to domestic company - Held, yes [Para 3.1] [In favour of revenue]

Section 11, read with  section 11B, of the Sebi Act, 1992 and section  8  of the Right to Information Act, 2005 -  Powers and Functions of Board  - Appellant filed a complaint with SEBI in relation to an allegation that in allocation of Offer for Sale (OFS) of respondent no.3 company, a major chunk of shares under OFS was allocated to related parties - SEBI informed appellant that after investigation, it was observed that 97 per cent of total allocation of OFS was to domestic mutual funds and that data did not corroborate with allegations in complaint - With respect to allegation of insider trading, complaint was forwarded to concerned division for their information and necessary action - Later, appellant filed an application under RTI Act seeking information regarding status and details of investigation - CPIO of SEBI vide RTI reply conveyed that information received through complaints was treated as market intelligence and information so received was analysed and if found necessary, further action was taken - It was also conveyed that any regulatory actions, if taken, were published on SEBI website - On appeal, First Appellate Authority noted that all complaints lodged in SCORES portal and related correspondence and action history could be accessed online on said portal under tab ‘View Complaint Status’ - First Appellate Authority concluded that maintenance of confidentiality of examination/investigation was of paramount importance since reports of same might result in unwarranted speculation or concern in market or might affect evidence collection during examination/investigation or might even result in unnecessary harm to third parties - Single Judge by impugned order dismissed writ petition filed by appellant holding that information regarding status of her complaint was duly provided to her; and information regarding internal investigation was exempted under section 8(1)(h) - It was noted that appellant only sought status of her complaint and not nature of investigations which, according to statutory authorities, was already on SCORES portal - Whether apart from status of complaint, nature of investigations even if sought by appellant stood exempted and thus could not be disclosed - Held, yes - Whether therefore, there was no reason to interdict impugned order - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12]

I. Section 2(22), read with sections 10(34), 115-O, 195 and 201, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Articles 10 and 13 of DTAA between India and Mauritius - Deemed dividend (Buy Back of Share Capital gains) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether profit arising out of buy back of shares of a corporate entity cannot be characterized as deemed dividend and same had to be taxed under head 'capital gains' - Held, yes - Whether under article 13 of India-Mauritius DTAA, capital gains on buy back of shares is not taxable in hands of non-resident recipient - Held, yes [Para 5.2] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Profit arising out of buy back of shares of a corporate entity is not 'deemed dividend' and it is to be taxed under head 'capital gains'; under article 13 of India-Mauritius DTAA, capital gains on buy back of shares is not taxable in hands of non-resident recipient  IT/ILT : If a company enters into a buy back deal of its shares without violating any provision of Act, merely because it results in non-payment or lesser payment of taxes, same will not be a colourable device to evade tax

I Section  9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with articles 7 and 12 of DTAA between India and USA - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India (Fee for technical services) - Assessment years 2007-08 and 2008-09 - Assessee-company, engaged in manufacture of pharmaceutical products, made payment to a US contract research organisation (CRO) for conducting clinical trials of its products and submit their reports -Whether since Applicant,had only provided final results to its Indian clients by using highly sophisticated bio-analytical know-how, without providing any access whatsoever to clients to such know-how, fee received by it was business income and not fee for technical/included services or royalty - Held, yes - Whether further applicant having no PE in India, such income would not be taxable in India by virtue of relevant provisions of DTAA - Held, yes [Para 58] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : In absence of making available of technical skill, knowledge or technical expertise or plans by conducting trial by CRO in U.S. to Indian company, payment made by Indian company was not fee for technical services  IT/ILT : Where assessee had granted loan to its subsidiary in Cyprus and received interest which was taxable in both countries, assessee was entitled to deduction of tax deemed to have been paid on interest income in Cyprus under article 25(2) of DTAA between India and Cyprus  IT/ILT : Assessing Officer should have charged ALP interest at LIBOR + 2 per cent on loans advanced by assessee to its subsidiary in different countries and not on basis of interest on unrelated corporate Bonds in India

Section  56  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income from other sources  -  Chargeable as  (Share premium) - Assessment year  2015-16  - Assessee-company issued further equity shares to its existing shareholders at Rs. 1777 per share based on valuation carried out by a Registered Valuer and Chartered Accountant, wherein market value of land, building and other tangible assets was determined at Rs. 462.99 crores and value of brand ‘HYATT’ was estimated at Rs. 26 crores and fair value of shares was computed at Rs. 1776 per share - Assessing Officer rejected valuation adopted under Explanation (ii) to section 56(2)(viib), changed method of valuation to Explanation (i) read with rule 11UA and determined fair value at Rs. 398 per share - Whether since genuineness of transaction had been established by identifying parties, transfer of funds through banking channels and utilisation for repayment of ECB loan and term loan, section 56(2)(viib) was not applicable as undisputedly Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals) had not made out a case of unaccounted money being infused and hence in absence of primary criteria, normal business transactions cannot be visited with rigours of section 56(2)(viib) -Held, yes - Whether since shares were issued to Non-resident shareholders at same price as that of resident shareholders, which had not been disputed by RBI and Assessing Officer, lower authorities could not adopt differential pricing only for resident shareholders - Held,yes - Whether Assessing Officer could not adopt a different method of valuation from one adopted by assessee nor reject valuation without demonstrating any defect in approach of Registered Valuer and thus, valuation determined by assessee based on market approach deserved acceptance and addition under section 56(2)(viib) was liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 9.2, 9.5, 15.4, 15.5, 16.20 and 17.3 to 17.6] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Interest) - Assessment years 2017-18 and 2018-19 - Assessee had made investment in preference shares issued by its UAE based subsidiary company - Excess share application money was refunded to assessee - TPO recharacterised said investment as loan advanced to AE and made TP adjustment by imputing interest thereon - Whether since amount was refunded before allotment of preference shares and transaction of subscription of preference shares itself was not found to be bogus or sham, adjustment made by TPO was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 14.5] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had made investment in preference shares issued by its UAE based subsidiary company and transaction of subscribing to preference shares of AE was not found to be bogus or sham, adjustment made by TPO imputing interest thereon by treating same as loan was to be deleted  TRANSFER PRICING : Where ALP adopted by assessee at LIBOR plus 200 basis points was accepted by Tribunal in earlier years, since no distinguishing feature was pointed out by revenue, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in adopting same in impugned year as well  TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee provided management consultancy services (MCS), technical services and business support services (BSS) to its AE, a company engaged in business of manufacture of electrical equipments was to be excluded from list of comparables being functionally different  TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee provided MCS, technical services and BSS to its AE, a company engaged in business of providing psychological assistance and counselling to employees in areas of prevention of sexual harassment, lifestyle management for shift employees, healthy maternity program etc. was incomparable to assessee  TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee provided MCS, technical services and BSS to its AE, a company engaged in business of development of specialized software was functionally incomparable to assessee  TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee's turnover was Rs. 13.99 crores, a company having turnover of Rs. 1.34 crores only was to be excluded from list of comparables failing turnover filter of 10 per cent  TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee provided MCS, technical services and BSS to its AE, a company providing market research and surveys, updating of data bases and admin support services was functionally comparable to assessee  TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee provided MCS, technical services and BSS to its AE, a company providing lifecycle management and human resources support services, data verification, processing of orders, telemarketing, monitoring quality of calls and call centers, payroll processing etc. was functionally comparable to assessee-company  TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had given corporate guarantee to its AEs for availing loans from financial institutions, in view of Tribunal's decision in assessee's own case for earlier assessment years guarantee commissioner charged accepting yield spread approach and also splitting of interest differential in ratio of 50:50 as done by assessee, same was to be upheld in impugned year as well

Section 90 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 26 of DTAA between India and France - Double taxation relief - Where agreement exists (Non-discrimination clause) - Assessment year 2020-21 - Whether higher rate of tax prescribed for foreign company is not to be regarded as violation of non-discriminatory clause, i.e., article 26 of DTAA between India-France - Held, yes [Para 14] [In favour of revenue]

Section 90 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 26 of DTAA between India and France - Double taxation relief - Where agreement exists (Non-discrimination clause) - Assessment year 2021-22 - Whether higher rate of tax prescribed for foreign company is not to be regarded as violation of non-discriminatory clause, i.e., article 26 of DTAA between India-France - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of revenue]

Section 253, read with section 172, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Appellate Tribunal - General - Assessment year 2010-11 - Whether tax effect in a 'case' means overall tax effect in respect of disputed issues in a particular assessment year - Held, yes - During previous year 40 voyages were undertaken by a French shipping company through its Indian agent and 40 returns were filed - Instead of passing 40 orders, a composite assessment order under section 172(4) was passed by Assessing Officer assessing total income at Rs. 2.72 crore - Whether since tax effect under appeal in instant case was more than stipulated tax effect of Rs. 3 lakhs, even though 30 out of 40 appeals had tax effects of less than Rs. 3 lakhs each, all 40 appeals were maintainable before Tribunal - Held, yes [Para 11] [In favour of revenue]

Section 11 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 - Power and functions of Board - Defendant company was a brokerage house and was a corporate member of Bombay Stock Exchange and National Stock Exchange of India - Applicant had alleged that defendant invited deposits through its business partner 'Crefin' and guaranteed return on capital and on such assurance, it invested a sum of Rs. 5.80 crore with defendant - Defendant acknowledged receipt of said amount by issuing 'welcome letters' and undertook obligation to pay interest - Initially, defendant did pay interest at agreed rate - Later on, applicant were in pressing need of funds and hence, sought refund of principal amount - Defendant not only committed default in refunding invested amount but also stopped payment of interest - Hence, applicant instituted suit for recovery of principal amount with interest - Defendant filed an affidavit in reply and sought an unconditional leave to defend suit on ground that there was no privity of contract whatsoever between applicant and defendant - Further, defendant never had any relationship either commercial or otherwise with said 'Crefin' - Welcome letters, which allegedly constitute contract, were forged and appeared to have been issued by one 'AS' who though was affiliated to defendant as its franchisee, but had no authority to issue and sign said letters on its behalf - Further, no amount deposited by applicant had been credited in account of defendant - Whether issues raised by defendant in its defence were triable issues and appeared to be a fair and reasonable defence, if not a positively good defence - Held, yes - Whether thus, defendant was entitled to an unconditional leave to defend suit - Held, yes [Para 29]COMPANY LAW/SEBI : Where in a suit filed by applicant for recovery of amount invested by it with defendant-brokerage house, defendant filed an affidavit raising triable issues such as, there was no privity of contract between parties, no amount was invested by applicant with defendant and documents, which had been relied upon by applicant to buttress their case of contract with defendant, were forged, since, defence of defendant appeared to be a fair and reasonable defence, defendant was entitled to an unconditional leave to defend suit

VII. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Health care/pharma supplies services) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee-company was engaged in providing software development services on a contractual basis - A comparable company was engaged in manufacturing and supply of medicines and also engaged in biopharma and biotech manufacturing and customized IT solutions, manufacture of drugs, clinical trials and contract research activities - This company was also into cloning and purification and industrial biotechnology area and manufacturing enzymes, alpha amylase and alkaline protease - Whether said company could not be accepted as valid comparable - Held, yes [Paras 44 and 45] [In favour of assessee]

III. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price - (Comparables, functional similarity - Manufacturer) - Assessment year : 2007-08 - Whether a company who is engaged in clinical research and manufacture of bio products and other products cannot be held comparable to assessees engaged in software development services business - Held, yes (para 12.iii) [In favour of Assessee]

I. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustment - Interest) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Whether where assessee company gave certain amount to its wholly owned subsidiary company as share application money, it could not be regarded as loan or advance till allotment of shares and, thus, impugned adjustment of notional interest made by revenue authorities deserved to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 14][In favour of assessee]IT/ILT-I : Where assessee company gave certain amount to its wholly owned subsidiary company as share application money, it could not be regarded as loan or advance till allotment of shares and, thus, impugned adjustment of notional interest made by revenue authorities deserved to be set aside  IT/ILT-II : Where assessee manufactured a pharmaceutical product for its AE on contract basis, in view of fact that assessee did not undertake any other functions namely marketing, distribution, credit risk, product litigation liabilities etc., ALP of transaction in question was to be determined on basis of TNMM  IT/ILT-III : Following order passed by Tribunal in assessee's own case relating to earlier assessment year, it was to be held that amount invested in OFCD of AE in respect of which option was not exercised to convert same into equity for a period of five years, no addition could be made on account of notional interest

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparability factors - Related party transactions) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee-company, engaged in manufacture and sale of pharmaceutical products, also undertook co-ordination of clinical trial services - Whether since selected company had significant RPT being much in excess of 25 per cent of total revenue as per its financials, it could not be accepted as a comparable - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]

Section 111 of the Companies Act, 1956, read with Regulation 11 of the Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer or Issue of Security by a Person Resident Outside India) Regulations, 2000 (FEMR) - Transfer of shares and debentures - Power to refuse registration and appeal against refusal - Whether, in terms of section 41(2), nobody can become a member of company unless he has agreed in writing to that effect - Held, yes - Whether where an NRI remitted funds in favour of one SN in India for incorporation and promotion of respondent-company and correspondence between them relating to memorandum and articles of association, receipt of the funds, constitution of the Board of Directors, requisition of business details, receipt and payment account, formalities in regard to patent registration and authority given to petitioner’s (NRI) father and brother in relation to affairs of company showed that petitioner had always intended to invest in company so as to carry on software business with SN, such correspondence would indicate that petitioner had agreed in writing to invest in company and that petitioner would be issued shares of company at an appropriate and mutually agreeable premium - Held, yes - Whether it was in compliance with requirement of section 41(1) - Held, yes - Whether where, though certificate of chartered accountant of respondent showed that premium per share was arrived at by mutual agreement between respondent and petitioner, there was no record to either substantiate any such mutual agreement between parties or due compliance with guidelines issued by Controller of Capital Issues in valuation of impugned shares, allotment of impugned shares in favour of petitioner was irregular and not in consonance with relevant provisions of FEMR and, therefore, respondent was to be directed to rectify register of members and delete name of petitioner in respect of impugned shares - Held, yes

Section 115A, read with section 195, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with Article 12 of DTAA between India and U.K - Foreign companies - Tax an dividends, royalty and technical services (Interest) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee, a UK resident, invested in an upcoming project of Omaxe in India - It had made payment of 95 per cent of sale price and was provisionally allotted floors in a proposed commercial complex in lieu of such 95 per cent advance payment, and Omaxe was to pay assured return on monthly basis to assessee till possession of commercial space was handed over - Such payment was made by Omaxe from assessment year 2008-09 to assessment year 2012-13 after deduction of tax under section 195 at rate 15 per cent under India U.K. Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) - Assessing Officer, however, was of view that assured return received by assessee was not interest income, rather he treated same as return from investment - It was found that assessee did not get right of lien in proposed property and had a claim of debt against Omaxe, which meant that assessee had advanced money to Omaxe which was nothing but a debt claim till proposed property would be constructed, executed and registered - Whether, on facts, it was a financial transaction and assured money return was nothing else than interest and therefore, Omaxe had rightly deducted tax at rate 15 per cent of interest/assured return paid to assessee [Para 11] [In favour of assessee]

III. Section 90 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 26 of DTAA between India and France - Double taxation relief - Where agreement exists (Non-discrimination clause) - Assessment years 2017-18 and 2018-19 - Whether in view of decision in assessee's own case in ACIT v. BNP Paribas [IT Appeal No. 7458 (Mum.) of 2018, dated 4-1-2021], higher rate of tax prescribed for foreign company is not to be regarded as violation of non-discriminatory clause, i.e., article 26 of DTAA between India-France - Held, yes [Paras 4, 7 and 8] [In favour of revenue]

I Section 56, read with section section 2(24) and 68, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income from other sources - Chargeable as (Share premium) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Whether section 56(2)(viib) read with section 2(24)(xvi) have applicability to receipt of consideration towards shares from resident entities and have no application when consideration towards shares are received from non-resident entities which are excluded in order to encourage foreign investments - Held, yes - Assessee, manufacturer of sale of footwear, was promoted by two foreign companies which were its shareholders - During relevant previous year, assessee had issued 41 lakh equity shares at consideration price of Rs. 20 per equity shares consisting of face value of Rs. 10 of each equity share and premium of Rs. 10 for each equity shares to its non-resident holding companies - Assessing Officer had invoked provisions of section 56(1) and additions were made in hands of assessee towards share premium charged by assessee - Further, Assessing Officer had tried to bring this amount under section 68 on ground that share premium charged was in excess of intrinsic valuation of shares because assessee was not only required to explain 'source' of credit entry but also its 'nature' which assessee could not explain - It was found that assessee had supported fair value of equity shares being Rs. 20 per equity share as against face value of Rs. 10 per equity share with a certificate issued by a chartered accountant using DCF method which was approved method as prescribed by RBI and assessee had filed its bank statements as well as FIRC issued by its bankers as evidence and thus, no fault lay with assessee in issuing equity shares - Whether, therefore, no addition was warranted towards share premium received by assessee from its holding companies as said share premium was on account of capital transaction and was not an income within charging sections of Act - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]IT : Section 56(2)(viib) read with section 2(24)(xvi) are not made applicable to shares issued to non-residents mainly to encourage foreign investments

Section 45, of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with article 13 of DTAA between India and Mauritius (Capital gains) - Chargeable as - Armstrong-Mauritius is a wholly owned subsidiary of Armstrong UK - Armstrong India was incorporated as fully owned subsidiary of Inarco, an Indian company - Armstrong Mauritius was holding 50 per cent shareholding of Inarco India - Pursuant to scheme of amalgamation, Inarco India transferred its flooring business to Armstrong India - Inarco India was allotted 3600 shares of Armstrong India - Subsequently, share capital of Inarco India was reduced by cancelling 50 per cent of its share capital - As consideration, Inarco India transferred shares of Armstrong India to Armstrong Mauritius - Now Armstrong India wants to buy back some of its shares from Armstrong Mauritius - No material is placed to justify that Armstrong Mauritius or Armstrong UK has devised a scheme for avoidance of tax - Whether though Armstrong Mauritius was incorporated and investment was made through it for acquiring shares of Indian company to take advantage of Indo-Mauritius DTAC, but that by itself was no ground to discard claim of applicant for benefit under Indo Mauritius DTAC - Held, yes - Whether capital gains could be taxed in Mauritius alone and, not taxable in India - Held, yes [In favour of applicant]

Section 56, read with section 2(18), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income from other sources - Chargeable as (Share premium) - Assessment year 2015-16 - During year, assessee-company issued shares at premium of Rs. 990 per share - Assessee contended that company was free to determine its own price with intending purchaser after due negotiations and deliberations - Assessing Officer did not accept contention of assessee and determined share premium under rule 11UA(1)(b) at Rs. 741 per share and, accordingly, added excess share premium collected to income of assessee by invoking provisions of section 56(2)(viib) - Whether since Assessing Officer had acknowledged fact that assessee was second level subsidiary of a company in which public was substantially interested, assessee's case would not fall under section 56(2)(viib), and, thus, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was unjustified - Held, yes [Paras 11 to 11.2] [In favour of assessee]IT: Where Assessing Officer made additions to income of assessee-company by invoking provisions of section 56(2)(viib) in respect of excess share premium received by it, since assessee was second level subsidiary of a company in which public was substantially interested, assessee's case would not fall under section 56(2)(viib), thus, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was unjustified  IT: Difference between value of actual investment and value as on balance sheet is not dividend income and, hence, section 14A could not be invoked

Section 6  of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, read with regulation 6 of the Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer of Issue of Security by a Person Resident Outside India) Regulations, 2000 - Capital account transactions - FMO, a Dutch company had paid Rs. 418 crores to Vinca Developer for purchase of shares and compulsorily convertible debentures (CCDs) - Defendant owned 49 per cent of voting rights in Vinca - Amount invested by FMO was used in purchasing OPCDs in a building construction project - Upon conversion of CCDs, FMO had become 99 per cent holder of Vinca - In respect of liability arising under OPCDs, defendant executed a deed of Corporate Guarantee in favour of plaintiff-IDBI who was debenture trustee of debentures issued to Vinca - Defendants failed to pay amounts due and payable and, therefore, plaintiff issued a demand certificate for enforcement of guarantee - Single Judge held that routing of FMO's FDI amount of Rs. 418 crores to Vinca was a colourable device to enable FMO to secure repayment (through Vinca) of its FDI amount and interest thereon at 14.75 per cent, contrary to statutory FEMA Regulations and FDI policy embodied therein - Whether since defendant had utilized amount invested by FMO, defence raised by defendants for non-payment was in realm of being 'plausible but improbable' - Held, yes - Whether defendant would be granted leave to defend suit only if it deposited in Bombay High Court principal sum of Rs. 418 crores invested by FMO, or gave security for said amount of Rs. 418 crores, to satisfaction of Prothonotary and Senior Master, Bombay High Court - Held, yes - Whether thus, appeal was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 20]FEMA: Where defendant had utilized amount invested by FMO, a Dutch company under a debenture trust deed, defendant would be granted leave to defend suit filed by debenture trustee on non-payment of amount only if it deposited in Court principal sum invested by FMO

Section  56 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with rule  11UA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 -  Income from other sources -  Chargeable as (Share premium) - Assessment year  2016-17 - During relevant year, assessee issued 97,200 equity shares of face value ?10 at a premium of ?2,562 per share - For computing FMV under section 56(2)(viib), assessee opted for Explanation (a)(ii), i.e., valuation based on assets including intangible assets - Immovable property was valued at circle rate as per approved valuer’s report, while unquoted shares held in investee companies were valued at book value as per their audited balance sheets - Assessing Officer accepted property valuation but rejected share valuation and recomputed FMV, making addition under section 56(2)(viib) - It was noted that assessee had taken FMV valuation relying upon data available in audited/ published financials of respective corporate entities - Whether value of unquoted equity shares investment held by assessee had been correctly calculated and, thus, order of Commissioner (Appeals) did not require any disturbance - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

Held: In the instant case there can be no doubt that the return from the investments is a return on a part of the paid up capital of the Company which is invested for the purpose of earning an income. (Para 6).

III. Section 56 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with rule 11UA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Income from other sources - Chargeable as (Sub-section (2)(viia)) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether where entire reserves and surplus appearing in balance sheet of company were only on account of grant/subsidy received from Government of India and not on basis of any business profit earned by company, said amount could not be taken into account while determining fair market value of shares as per provisions of section 56(2)(viia), read with rule 11UA - Held, yes [Para 26] [In favour of assessee]

Section 4, read with section 9 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Chargeable as (Tax planning/Tax avoidance) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was a limited company engaged in business of manufacturing, trading and exporting drugs and pharmaceutical products - It had six business premises located at Mumbai - Assessing Officer found that assessee had several subsidiaries in India and Outside India - One of subsidiary company of assessee namely Sun BVI transferred certain technologies to CARACO, USA over a certain period - Sun BVI acquired those technologies from UTL, another subsidiary of assessee which allegedly acquired those technologies from assessee - Cost of technologies in hand of Sun BVI was very nominal in comparison to value at which Sun BVI transferred it to CARACO - As such Sun BVI earned huge profit margin on those transactions which was exempt from tax as Sun BVI was located in a tax heaven zone - In course of assessment, Assessing Officer took a view that UTL was only a paper company which did not develop any technology - He further opined that technologies were developed by assessee and thereupon those technologies were transferred to CARACO, USA routed through UTL only to evade payment of tax in India - Assessing Officer thus concluded that profit arising from transfer of technologies was liable to tax in India in hands of assessee - It was noted from records that UTL was very much engaged in development activity of technology but indirectly as job worker, thus, role of UTL in development of technology could not be ruled out completely - As regards SUN BVI, it was seen that said company was registered in tax heaven in British virgin Islands and, since, said company was not resident in India under section 6(3), income earned by it was not taxable in India - It was also noticed that CARACO, USA, had paid sale consideration to Sun BVI, by issuing shares, prices of which increased manifold after transfer of technologies, however, it was not possible to predict price of shares in future at time of delivery of technology and, therefore, increase in price of shares could not be held as colourable device in hands of Sun BVI - Whether in view of aforesaid, impugned transaction could not be regarded as colourable device merely on reasoning that there was no tax liability arising in hands of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, consequently, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 19.4 to 19.16] [In favour of assessee]SLD : Where subsidiary of assessee-company located in tax heaven country transferred a new technology to US based company after acquiring it from another subsidiary of assessee located in India, profit arising from said transaction was not taxable in India  INTERNATIONAL TAXATION : Where one subsidiary of assessee-company developed a new technology in pharmaceutical business and transferred same to another subsidiary of assessee located in tax heaven country, which in turn transferred said technology to a US based company, profit arising from transaction in question was not liable to tax in India

facts.text:
Information Technologies (P.) Ltd., Singapore and Teledata Informatics Ltd., Chennai. This agreement could not be implemented due to the fraud perpetrated upon 'V' and Esys Information Technologies Pte., Singapore by Teledata Informatics.

In the counter affidavit, it was contended that rule 9 had not been technically violated by the respondent. Though, the respondent's shareholding pattern had undergone a change after allotment but it could not be a ground for the resumption of the allotment. Along with the rejoinder, the appellant had filed two affidavits filed by 'V' in the High Court of Republic of Singapore in Suit. It was submitted that the holding company was the Singapore Company and Dubai and India based companies were its subsidiary companies. The allotment was made in favour of Esys Information Technologies. Esys, Singapore could not have transferred assets as per clause 15 of the allotment order for a period of ten years. The stake of Dubai company by virtue of 95 per cent shares transfer had raised to 98 per cent. Esys Global Holdings Ltd., Dubai further sold these stakes to Teledata, a Chennai based company. Facts stated in affidavit dated 2-7-2008 of 'V' which was part of the record of the Estate Officer had been concealed in spite of the categorical order dated 16-7-2015 passed by the Supreme Court. The way in which the transaction had been made was a transfer which was not permissible as per rules and conditions of allotment letter. In fact there was transfer of plot from one company to the other company. The respondent was using the land for increasing valuation of assets and thereby improving financial worth. The holding company and its subsidiaries were two distinct legal entities. The Court should lift the veil so as to unearth mala fide, dishonest and fraudulent design of the respondent. Teledata was claiming to have acquired Esys Singapore and showing the plot in question as its asset.

Facts

SBL was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, having its registered office in India.

ShanH, a French company, held 80 per cent shares of SBL.

The shares of ShanH were held by two French companies namely MD and GIMA alongwith a person namely 'H'.

A share purchase agreement (SPA) was entered into between MD/GIMA and Sanofi, a French company, in terms of which shares of ShanH were transferred to Sanofi.

MA and GIMD applied for advance ruling to AAR. The AAR ruled that the transaction involved in the SPA was only for acquisition of the control, management and business interests in SBL, the Indian company and was not a mere divestment of ShanH shares, a French company. As a result, capital assets in India were transferred and capital gains had accrued to MA/GIMD, in India. The transaction was held to be taxable in India since that right was allocated to India, under Article 14(5) of the India-France DTAA.

Sanofi was also held assessee in default for non-deduction of tax at source under section 195 while making payments to MA and GIMD.

The three companies i.e. MA, GIMD and Sanofi filed separate writ petitions challenging the order passed by the AAR.

Issues involved

(1)

Was ShanH not an entity with commercial substance; was it a sham or illusory contrivance, a mere nominee of MA and/or MA/GIMD being the real, legal and beneficial owner(s) of SBL shares; and a device incorporated and pursued only for the purpose of avoiding capital gains liability under the Act?

(2)

Was the investment, initially by MA and thereafter by MA and GIMD through ShanH in SBL, a colourable device designed for tax avoidance? If so, whether the corporate veil of ShanH must be lifted and the transaction (of the sale of the entirety of ShanH shares by MA/GIMD to Sanofi) treated as a sale of SBL shares?

(3)

Was the transaction, liable to tax in India?

(4)

Whether retrospective amendments to provisions of the Act (by the Finance Act, 2012) after the trajectory or impact provisions of the DTAA and/or otherwise render the transaction liable to tax under the provisions of the Act?

(5)

Whether the AAR ruling was sustainable?

(6)

Whether the order determining the petitioner-Sanofi to be an 'assessee in default' in respect of payments made by it to MA and GIMD for acquisition of ShanH shares, under section 201(1) was valid?

• MBT (TM) was set-up in India under a joint venture agreement between M&M and BT. The applicant company was incorpoarated in Mauritius. Its 57% shareholder company was a wholly owned subsidiary of M & M and the remains 43% per cent shareholder company was BT.

• In connection with two multi party Option Agreements' to allot shares of MBT, involving the applicant company, and other company which appeared to be in circumvention of SEBI Guidelines, the issues before the Authority of Advance Ruling was :

- Whether question of legality or regularity of transaction or what may be called circumvention of SEBI Guidelines is inside the purview of Authority?

- Whether Authority has discretion to refuse a ruling on a transaction which it found to be on the basis of circumvention of a vital Guideline issue in public interest?

■

The company R was incorporated in the year 1991 by two non-resident Indians Dr. K and B along with S, the younger brother of Dr. K, and an Indian entrepreneur. The company took up a project to establish a hospital cum diagnostic centre at Calcutta. The project cost was about Rs. 11 crores. 88 per cent of the project, i.e. Rs. 8 crores were to be by way of NRI participation. The balance 11.12 per cent of the shares was to be contributed by resident Indians. The NRI investment was approved by the Department of industrial development, Government of India, Secretariat of Industrial Approval (SIA ). Dr. K was one of the 1st directors of the said company. He along with Dr. B held 52.74 per cent of the equity shares in the company. Dr. K contributed Rs. 4.26 crores out of which about Rs. 3.5 crores were by way of second-hand equipment brought from the USA. Sajal contributed Rs. 1.23 crores.

■

The Reserve Bank of India granted permission for allotment of shares to Dr. K for the equipment brought by him from the USA.

■

The writ petition filed by petitioner here was dismissed by the Single Judge.

■

On appeal;

■

The assessee, a non-resident company incorporated and registered in Cyprus, was engaged in the business of investment in shares and debentures of other companies and earned income through interest, dividend and appreciation in the value of investment. The assessee had invested in 66,030 compulsory convertible debentures (CCD) of Rs. 10,000 each in its Indian AE, an Indian company. The CCDs carried an interest rate of 17.75 per cent per annum. The assessee had earned interest of Rs. 13.02 crores on these CCDs and offered the same to tax on gross basis to be taxed at the rate of 10 per cent as per the provisions of article 11 of the DTAA between India and Cyprus.

■

During the course of scrutiny assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee had only earned interest income on CCDs from its AE which implied that the assessee company had made only one investment since its incorporation despite being an investment company. The Assessing Officer held that the assessee was not eligible for benefits under India-Cyprus DTAA. Hence, the benefit of India-Cyprus DTAA was disallowed and the income was taxed at the rate of 20 per cent under section 115A.

■

On appeal, the DRP also declined to interfere with the findings of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The petitioners were shareholders of Vinca holding 20.50 per cent of class-A equity shares each and 50 per cent of class-B equity shares each, whereas Dutch company FMO held 10 per cent class-A equity shares, i.e., 0.01 per cent of total share equity capital of Vinca and 3 CCDs (Compulsory Convertible Debentures) over a period of 60 months into 99 per cent of Class-A Equity Shares in Vinca. Whereas Respondent No. 5 Hubtown held 49 per cent of class-A equity shares amounting to 0.05 per cent of the total issue and paid up equity of Vinca.

The Petitioners invested Rs. 12.50 crores in Vinca. Thereafter, through a subscription agreement, FMO invested Rs. 418 crores. The petitioners claimed that the money FMO invested in Vinca towards equity share capital and CCDs and the proceeds were transferred contractually into its subsidiaries Amazia and Rubix to obtain fixed assured return in violation of FDI policies.

The petitioners further claimed that reserved matters and associated clauses provided in the Article of Association (AOA) of Vinca had been insinuated ensuring absolute control to FMO over all the matters relating to the CCDs, their conversion and also on the OPCDs (optionally partly convertible debentures) of Amazia and Rubix subscribed by Vinca to the exclusion of other shareholders.

FMO currently held 10 per cent of equity of Vinca through class-A shares and was entitled to 10 per cent of voting rights and economic interest in Vinca as also 3 CCDs in Vinca which upon conversion would entitle FMO to 99 per cent of the equity of Vinca, thereby entitling it to 99 per cent of the voting rights. Further, 49 per cent of equity of Vinca was owned by R-5 Hubtown and the rest 41 per cent class A equity shares were owned by the petitioners entitling them of respective percentage of voting rights. The petitioners also own 100 per cent of class B equity shares of Vinca.

The monies in Vinca invested by FMO were used by Vinca to subscribe to certain optionally partially convertible debentures (OPCDs) issued by Amazia and Rubix by execution of Debenture Subscription and Debenture Trustee Agreements making IDBI-Trusteeship services Ltd. (Respondent No. 10) as trustee. Vinca subscribed to the OPCDs as per the Trust Deeds. In order to secure the said OPCDs, the R-5 Hubtown inter alia vide the Corporate Guarantee Deed issued an unconditional, absolute and irrevocable corporate guarantee in favour of the debenture trustee inter alia for the benefit of Vinca. The option was left open to FMO to convert those OPCDs into shareholdings.

The debenture trustee issued redemption notices to Amazia and Rubix when they neglected to pay the amounts payable in terms of the Trust Deeds. Debenture trustee issued demand certificate for the enforcement of the guarantee to R-5 Hubtown. When no reply was received by the trustee, it filed a suit before the High Court which was transferred to the list of commercial causes cases against which the trustee appealed to the Supreme Court which directed R-5 Hubtown to deposit the principal sum of Rs. 418 crores invested by FMO in the Bombay High Court for defending the suit.

The petitioners claimed that the investment structure conceived by FMO for bringing foreign investment into Amazia and Rubix routing through Vinca was in breach of FEMA; therefore, the rights accrued to FMO on Rs. 418 crores invested in Vinca should not be exercised and all such rights vested in FMO should be set aside by holding that FMO exercising its rights for realization of its money as oppressive against the petitioners.

The assessee-company had made outward investment in Emirates of Ajman in the form of a Free Zone Entity (FZE) 'Vega' in the Ajman Free Zone. The income earned through the said establishment had not been shown as income of the assessee-company in the books of the assessee. Since in this entity, the assessee was the sole shareholder having 100 per cent shareholding, the assessee was asked to explain the legal status of this entity and to explain how this entity was legally independent entity managed and controlled wholly from UAE. In reply the assessee submitted that the memorandum of incorporation of company Vega clearly certified that this FZE with limited liability was established as corporate entity and independent and separate financial liability from those of its owner and, therefore, it was clearly established that it was a company, which was having its own separate entity independent stature and had its separate financial liability. The Assessing Officer was not satisfied. He came to the conclusion that the entity did not have separate legal identity vis-Ã-vis its sole shareholder and for any non-compliance, the owner was responsible legally whereas in Indian Companies Act, 1956 shareholders are not legally liable for any act of the company or its board of directors. On that basis, the Assessing Officer treated the income of the Vega as income taxable in India in the hands of the assessee under section 5(1).

On appeal:

The applicant, claimed to be a non-resident company in UAE, held more than 10 per cent of the shares of a limited company of Bombay. It was also said to be holding shares of other companies in India and to be in the process of acquiring more than 10 per cent of the shares of certain other companies. The applicant moved an application for advance ruling under section 245Q(1) claiming to be entitled to the benefit under article 10(2)(a) of DTAA with UAE, according to which tax charged on dividend shall not exceed 5 per cent of the gross amount of the dividend if the beneficial owner is a company which owns at least ten per cent of the shares of the company paying the dividend. These facts gave rise to a preliminary objection to the entertainment of application. The objection was that, as there was no company law or law regarding corporations in the UAE and the applicant was only a trade name for an individual XYZ, who owned the business of the applicant, and that since this individual was resident in India in the financial year 1994-95 within the meaning of section 6(1)(a) , the application was not maintainable.

One 'MA' is an International Health Care Group incorporated in France. It formed a wholly owned subsidiary in France named 'ShanH'. It entered into a share purchase agreement acquiring the shares of an Indian company, called Shantha. The shares in Shantha were acquired by ShanH. Subsequently, applicant came into the picture by acquiring 20 per cent shares from MA in ShanH. With a view to ensuring the achievement of better progress in business by Shantha, a commercial transaction was evolved whereby Sanofi, another company incorporated in France, came forward to participate actively with MA and applicant. With a view to further improve the business and performance, MA and applicant sold their shares in ShanH to Sanofi in August, 2009. Thereupon, MA and applicant filed instant applications before this authority under section 245Q(1) seeking an advance ruling on the following question.

Whether in terms of the provisions of the India-France DTAA read with section 90, the capital gains arising from the sale of shares of ShanH by the applicant to Sanofi (French Incorporated Entity) is liable to tax in France or in India?

On 4-3-1995, a company BCL (subsequently as ICL) was formed by the Birla group. On 5-12-1995, US company AT&T and a Birla group company Grasim entered into a Joint Venture Agreement ('JVA'), under which, BCL was to be the Joint Venture Company ('JVC'). Under the joint venture, 51 per cent equity shares of the JVC were to be subscribed and owned by the Birla group and 49 per cent of the equity shares of the JVC were to be subscribed and owned by AT&T-US. Under the JVA, the AT&T-US as a founder was to own and hold 49% equity shares in BCL. Under the JVA, the equity shares subscribed by the founders as party shareholders could be issued in the name of a permitted transferee which was a 100 per cent subsidiary of the founder. AT&T-Mauritius being a 100 per cent subsidiary of AT&T-US was eligible to hold 49 per cent equity shares of JVC as a permitted transferee of the AT&T-US. Accordingly, AT&T-US subscribed to the shares of the JVC and equity shares of the JVC were allotted in the name of AT&T-Mauritius, as a permitted transferee of AT&T-US. Though the equity shares were issued in the name of AT&T-Mauritius under the JVA as a permitted transferee of AT&T-US, all rights in respect of the said equity shares of the JVC like voting rights, rights of management, right of sale or alienation, etc., absolutely vested in AT&T-US.

In October 1997, AT&T-Mauritius and the Birla group executed a document titled as 'confirmation with respect to closing of Joint Venture Agreement'. AT&T-Mauritius was neither a party to the JVA nor was it obliged to pay any amount under the JVA to hold the equity shares of ICL as a permitted transferee of AT&T-US. However, the liability of AT&T-US to pay for the equity shares of the JVC were discharged by AT&T-Mauritius during the period from 1996 to 2003.

Later on Tata group company 'TCL' merged and JVC was restructured. On the other hand, Cingular Wireless of USA acquired shares of AT&T Wireless of USA from AT&T, USA and renamed it as 'NCWS'.

The assessee was a company incorporated in, and fiscally domiciled in, the Republic of Mauritius. It holds a global business licence (GBL) issued by the Financial Services Commission, Mauritius.
