1.1-8 DIVERSIFICATION OF ACTIVITIES/SET UP STEP DOWN SUB-SIDIARIES/ALTERATION OF SHAREHOLDING PATTERN BY OVERSEAS WOS/JV WITHOUT THE RBI’S PRIOR APPROVAL - The Indian party should report to the RBI the details of such decisions taken by JV/WOS within 30 days of the approval of such decisions by the competent authority concerned under the local laws of the host country and include the same in annual APR to be forwarded to the RBI annually.

1.1-9 OBLIGATIONS OF THE INDIAN PARTY WHICH HAS MADE DIRECT INVESTMENTS OUTSIDE INDIA - Such a company has to :

(i) Receive copies of share certificate or any other document issued by JV/WOS evidencing investment from the Indian party within 6 months of the date of remittance or date on which amount to be capitalized became due or the date on which amount due was allowed to be capitalized.

(ii) Repatriate to India, all dues receivable from the foreign entity (dividend, royalty, technical fees, etc.) within 60 days of its falling due or within such extended time allowed by the RBI.

(iii) Submit to the RBI an Annual Performance Report in Form APR. This has to be done within 60 days from the date of expiry of the statutory period as prescribed by laws of the host country for finalisation of duly audited accounts or within such further period as may be allowed by the RBI.

1.1-10 INVESTMENT IN AGRICULTURAL OPERATIONS OVERSEAS - A person resident in India being a company incorporated in India or a partnership firm registered under the Indian Partnership Act may undertake agricultural operations including purchase of land incidental to such activity either directly or without the RBI’s prior approval if the eligibility conditions and limits discussed above are satisfied.

1.1-11 SALE OF SHARES OF AN OVERSEAS JV/WOS - Sale should be to another Indian party who complies with the eligibility conditions and limits for Automatic Route or to a person resident outside India. The following conditions should be satisfied:

(a) The sale does not result in write-off of investment made.

(b) The sale is effected through a stock exchange where shares of the overseas JV/WOS are listed.

(c) If the shares are not listed and disinvestment is by private arrangement, the share price is not less than the value certified by a CA/CPA as the fair value of the shares based on the latest audited financial statements of the JV/WOS.

(d) The Indian party does not have any outstanding dues (dividend, technical fees, royalty, consultancy, commission or export proceeds or other entitlements) from the JV/WOS.

(e) The overseas JV/WOS has been in operation for at least one full year and the APR together with audited accounts have been submitted to the RBI.

(f) The Indian party is not under investigation by the CBI/ED/SEBI/IRDA/any other regulatory authority in India.

Sale proceeds should be repatriated to India within 90 days from the date of sale and documentary evidence to this effect should be submitted to the RBI through designated AD.

17. Ofcourse the law of the land has to be complied with by all entities, whether foreign or domestic, but MNC in contradistinction to domestic companies, by definition, have the choice of not doing business in India. Having said this, it is also necessary to see what are some of the key issues involved, which are discussed under various heads below.

RBI valuation methodology for Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) into the country The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has prescribed rules under the Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer or Issue of Security by a Person Resident Outside India) Regulations, 2000 ("TISPRO Regulations"). Upto 3rd May 2010, the RBI methodology required the minimum price for unlisted shares issued to non-residents to be fixed based on the average of the Net Asset Value ("NAV") and the Profit Earning Capacity Value ("PECV") of the company, which were the methods prescribed under the erstwhile Controller of Capital Issues (CCI) Guidelines issued in 1990. These methods were based on historical figures appearing in the books of the Company. Effective 4th May 2010, the RBI has issued A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 49 in terms of which the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) method, based on the Company's future projected free cash flows in perpetuity discounted using its weighted average cost of capital, is used for fixing the minimum value to be brought into the country per share, for the total number of shares issued to the non-resident.

In the case of Shell India, since its downstream business was incurring loss, to fund which, capital was issued to Shell Netherlands in 2009, it is reasonable to presume that under the then prevalent RBI valuation guidelines (i.e. average of the Net Asset Value ("NAV") and the Profit Earning Capacity Value ("PECV")) based on the historical financials of the company, this valuation methodology would have resulted in a negative net worth or a sub-par value per share. Also, as per the information in the public domain, Shell India computed its DCF value per share at that time to be Rs.6.93. Since there were restrictions on issue of shares at a discount under section 79 of the Companies Act, 1956, the Shell India shares would have been issued at par i.e. at Rs. 10, to Shell Netherlands, which exceeded the floor price under the RBI Rules. Hence, for the purpose of FDI into the country, the applicable methodology under the RBI Rules would thus have been complied with by Shell India at the time it issued shares to Shell Netherlands.

Fair Market Valuation (FMV) under the IT Act

Section 56(2)(viia) has been introduced into the IT Act with effect from 1st June 2010 by the Finance Act, 2010 to tax the discount on the issue of shares of a closely held company (e.g. Shell India) received by another closely held company (e.g. Shell Netherlands) from any person (e.g. Shell India). The discount is computed as the difference between the fair market value of the shares –computed in the manner prescribed in rule 11UA(1)(c)(b) of the IT Rules which is based largely on the NAV method – and the consideration received against the shares issued. However, the Shell India/Netherlands share issue transaction which occurred in 2009 is not covered by this sub-section which came into the statute books subsequently.

There is also a view prevalent that this section applies only to a transfer of existing shares and not an allotment of new shares that the recipient receives for a consideration less than the FMV of these shares. This view however is not apparent from a plain reading of the section and relies on the Explanatory Memorandum in the Finance Bill, 2010 when this section was introduced in the IT Act (that refers to transfer of shares at less than their FMV), though it can be urged in arguments.

More than one valuation methodology possible for share valuation under IT Act

Section 56(2)(viia) effective 1st June 2010, read with rule 11UA(1)(c)(b) prescribes a NAV valuation methodology based on historical figures for determining the FMV of the shares of a closely held company received by another closely held company.

[Para 11] It is now quite well settled that the doctrine of piercing or removing corporate veil is applicable not only in the case of holding of subsidiary companies or in the case of tax evasion but can be equally applied in execution proceedings. The doctrine has been referred to also in cases:—

(i) Where 'two separate corporate entities are functioning as if they are in partnership with one company as an alter-ego of the other company, where one company is bound hand and foot by the other';

(ii) Where 'parent company's management has steering influence on the subsidiary's core activities that the subsidiary can no longer be regarded to perform those activities on the authority of its own exclusive directors'; and

(iii) Where 'the company is the creature of the group and the mask which is held before its face in an attempt to avoid recognition by the eye of equity or is a mere cloak or sham and in truth the business was being carried on by one person and not by the company as a separate entity'.

(iv) Where 'two companies are inextricably inter-linked corporate entities'.

Therefore, the concept of lifting of corporate veil is also available in execution proceedings. [Para 19]

Therefore the corporate veil can be lifted in cases where the Court from the material on record comes to the conclusion that the Judgment Debtor is trying to defeat the execution of the Award which is passed against him. The Single Judge was justified in carrying out that exercise. [Para 20]

The second question which falls for consideration is: whether the Single Judge was justified in lifting the corporate veil in instant case and whether the Single Judge was further justified in coming to the conclusion that BIIL and BIL was a single economic entity. [Para 21]

Respondent No. 2- Vitol S.A. ('Vitol') had obtained a London arbitral award on 17-1-2011 against Asian Natural Resources (India) Ltd. (Formerly Bhatia International Limited) ('BIL') for a sum of US $ 68,435,250—towards damages for breach of the Master Agreement together with interest thereon and legal costs. Respondent No. 2 filed execution proceedings in the Court and filed an application seeking an order of precept under section 46 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, seeking attachment 54,300 MT of coal at the Tuticorin Port at Tamil Nadu. Application was made by 'S' objecting to the attachment levied under the Judges Order 215 of 2014. The said application filed by 'S' was heard by the Single Judge and by judgment dated 2-9-2015 in Judges Order 215 of 2014 the Single Judge held that 34,300 MT of coal was under the ownership of 'S' and the remaining cargo was under the ownership of the Appellants/BIIL and directed Respondent No. 2 - Vitol to issue notice to BIIL inviting them to object to the attachment/extending the precept with respect to the remaining 34,300 MT of cargo. The Single Judge, after giving an opportunity to BIIL and BIL of being heard, came to the conclusion that BIIL and BIL was a single entity after going through the exercise of piercing veil of two companies and other group companies know as Bhatia Group. [Para 22]

In the application filed by respondent No. 2 - Vitol for attachment/extending the precept with respect to remaining coal, respondent No. 2 narrated the circumstances and facts which, according to them, disclose that BIIL and BIL was in fact a single entity. The Single Judge accepted the contention of respondent No. 2 - Vitol and has held that BIIL is indeed an alter-ego of BIL and they are one single unit and, therefore, though the property was in the name of BIIL, it was in fact the property of BIL and could be attached and sold in execution. [Para 23]

The Single judge has observed that BIIL and BIL was one single economic entity which was being managed by Bhatia and his close relatives. [Para 24]

The view taken by the Single Judge is concurred with. The Single Judge has considered all the circumstances which indicate that Bhatia and his members of his family had created several corporate bodies and they were controlled by Bhatia and his family and therefore the Single Judge has rightly come to the conclusion that they had to be treated as one single entity as they were being used as cloaks behind which Bhatia and his family were using the device of incorporation as ploy adopted for preventing execution of the international award which was passed against BIL and in favour of respondent. [Para 25]

Certainly, it will be preposterous to even suggest that HTIL-M, which is admittedly a non-resident associated enterprise, is not a party to the arrangements in question. Similarly, it is also not possible to even seriously suggest that VIH-BV, which is the ultimate parent company was not part of the arrangement in question. VIH-BV is not only a signatory and party to the FA 2007, SHA 2007, TA 2007 and Termination Deed 2011, it is the end beneficiary of all these arrangements. Once an entity is party to an agreement, it cannot be said that the said entity, even if it does not have any legal rights under the agreement, is not part of arrangement or understanding. An entity may be part of the arrangements with or without any enforceable legal rights. The correctness of statement, however, independent of the position whether or not such an entity may or may not have any enforceable legal rights, is evident from the statutory definition of transaction which states that 'transaction, includes any an arrangement, understanding or action in concert, (a) whether or not such arrangement, understanding or action is formal or in writing; or (b) whether or not such arrangement, understanding or action is intended to be enforceable by legal proceeding'. [Para 101]

Open offer by Sterlite for Acquisition of Shares of INDAL

Sterlite Industries (India) Limited and Eastern Galvanising Pvt. Limited (Sterlite) submitted a copy of the public announcement to SEBI as required under Regulation 15 of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 1997 (the Regulations) to acquire 71,11,200 shares comprising 10% of the paid up equity share capital of Indian Aluminium Company Limited (INDAL). The offer was conditional and was only for 10% of the paid up equity share capital of the largest company. The public announcement was scheduled to appear in the newspapers on February 19, 1998. The public announcement was exami-ned by SEBI with reference to the provisions of the Regulations and also keeping in view the paramount interest of the investors. The merchant bankers to the Sterlite and representatives of Sterlite as well as represen-tative of Indal and their merchant banker were called for a discussion.

The merchant banker to Sterlite put forth an interpretation of the Regulations to substantiate the conditional offer of 10% without offeringto acquire a minimum of 20%. From a harmonious reading of the various provisions of the Regulations, it emerged that the offer has to be for a minimum 20% of the paid up equity share capital of the company. Accordingly, the merchant banker representing Sterlite, the acquirer agreed to make an offer for acquisition of 20% of the paid up equity capital of the target company i.e., Indal, while retaining the clause relating to minimum acceptance level of 10%. This would mean that while on one hand Sterlite the acquirer, would make an offer to acquire 20%, the acquirer would be under no obligation to accept any shares if the response is less than 10%. On the other hand if the response is more than 10%, the acquirer i.e., Sterlite would be bound to accept whatever has been tendered in acceptance upto a 20%. This amendment to the public announcement is in the larger interest of investors so that they get an opportunity to participate in the offer to a larger extent and also reaffirm the principle of minimum offer of 20% which is central to the takeover regulations.

Order under Takeover Regulations

M/s. Nahar Investors and Traders Private Limited, the acquirer, filed an application before the Securities and Exchange Board of India seeking exemption from the application of Chapter III of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 1997 for acquisition upto 15% of the equity capital of M/s. Mahavir Spinning Mills Limited, the target company, from the open market.

As per the application the acquirer alongwith its associates and persons acting in concert currently holds 51% of the equity share capital/voting power in the target company. The exemption was sought on the grounds that the acquirers wish to consolidate their shareholding upto 15% of the shareholding in the Target Company with the intent to arrest the sharp fall in the price of the scrip which has been witnessed in the recent past and to infuse new faith and confidence in the minds of the shareholders.

The application also makes an alternate prayer to the Board that if the exemption sought is rejected, the acquirers should at least be excused from the minimum offer price stipulation under Regulation 20(2).

The application was forwarded by the Board to the Takeover Panel in terms of the provisions of sub-regulation (4) of Regulation 4 of the Regulations. The Panel considered the facts of the case in light of the objective intended to be achieved by the Takeover Code and recommended that the exemption sought may not be granted. Thereafter, in accordance with the provisions of sub-regulation (6) of Regulation 4, theacquirers were given an opportunity of a personal hearing on February 9, 1998 to present their case and make their submissions, if any.

After taking into consideration the recommendations of the Panel and the submissions made by the acquirers, SEBI has agreed with the recommendations of the Panel and rejected the exemption application and has directed the acquirers to abide by the public offer obligations under the Regulations if they are desirous of acquiring the proposed shares.

As per the scheme of arrangement, GGPL would cease to be a subsidiary of the petitioner since the holding of the petitioner in GGPL would vest in 'K'. The existing shareholders of the petitioner would continue to retain their shareholding in the petitioner. In addition, each shareholder would be given one share of 'K' for every four equity shares held in the petitioner. The scheme was not a scheme of amalgamation but a scheme where the investment held by the petitioner in a subsidiary was to be transferred to another company in which the existing shareholders of the petitioner would hold share pro rata to their holding in the petitioner. [Para 7]

Admittedly, for a period of two years GGPL, had not declared dividend. GGPL carried on capital intensive activities and its board of directors perhaps considered it appropriate to plough back the returns in the existing business. The commercial wisdom of the directors of GGPL in not declaring dividend did not fall for consideration in instant proceedings. The benefit which the petitioner sought to derive upon the transfer of its investment in GGPL to 'K' was to enable itself to focus on its core pharmaceutical business, improve its market position and enhance its own financial standing by divesting itself of the subsidiary whose financial position necessarily impinged upon the petitioner. From the chart produced before the Court, it would appear that for the financial year ending 31-3-2003, the ratio of profit before tax to net sales would be 12.2 without GGPL and 10.7 with GGPL; the debt/equity ratio would be 0.9 instead of 1.6; the return on the capital employed would be 31.2 per cent instead of 25.7 per cent and the return on net worth would be 30.9 per cent instead of 25.7 per cent. These were commercial considerations which had weighed with the board of directors of the petitioner and its shareholders in support of the scheme of arrangement. [Para 9]

The grievance of the objector that there ought to have been a valuation of the shares held in GGPL for determining the exchange ratio missed the point. The said scheme was not a scheme of amalgamation or merger. NPIL continued and would continue to exist even after the scheme was enforced. The existing shareholders of NPIL would continue as shareholders of NPIL. NPIL had an investment in GGPL, but so long as NPIL continued to exist as a corporate body and no shareholder had an identifiable share or right in the assets of NPIL. The holding of the petitioner in GGPL was to vest in 'K' under the scheme of arrangement. The existing shareholders of the petitioner would be allotted one equity share in 'K' for every four equity shares held in the petitioner. That was in addition to the existing holding in the petitioner. In reply to the objections it had been stated by the petitioner that the ratio was arrived at by taking into consideration that 'K' must have a minimum paid-up capital of Rs. 10 crores to facilitate the listing of its shares on the stock exchange. After excluding the initial paid-up capital of Rs. 5 lakh (i.e. 50,000 shares of Rs. 10 each) of 'K' which was the minimum required for the purpose of incorporating 'K' as a public limited company, the distribution of the balance 99.50 lakh shares (i.e., 100 lakh shares minus 0.50 lakh shares required for incorporation) of 'K' against 380 lakh shares of NPIL gave a fractional ratio of 1:3.82 shares, which ratio had been rounded off to 1:4. The shares of 'K' would be listed on the stock exchange and, thus, would provide an exit opportunity to a shareholder to sell his shares if he chose to do so. The ratio of 1:4 in which the shares of 'K' would be issued to the shareholders of the petitioner, would consume 95,00,801 shares. There would be a shortfall of 4,49,199 shares to make up the capital of Rs. 10 crores required for the listing of 'K'. The scheme provided that NPIL which was a wholly owned subsidiary of NPIL would subscribe for these 4,49,199 shares for cash at par. [Para 10]

The subject matter of the dispute was Joint Venture Agreement between the parties. The dispute between the parties arose consequent to meeting of Board when resolution was taken no to re-appoint Vikram Bakshi as Managing Director of CPRPL. Company Petition was filed thereafter by Vikram Bakshi which has been allowed. [Para 11]

The settlement application is being Opposed by HUDCO. The question which need to be considered in these Appeals is as to whether HUDCO has made sufficient ground to reject settlement application. [Para 12]

There is material on the record that insofar as 3100 shares held by Vikram Bakshi in CPRPL, the amount corresponding to the share value has already been deposited before the DRT, an amount of Rs. 10 Crores which has been withdrawn. [Para 16]

The contention which has been much pressed by the HUDCO is that the deposit of amount towards 3100 shares is not sufficient compliance of the order of the Recovery Officer. It is submitted that 50 per cent shareholding in CPRPL consisted of 1.06 per cent shareholding by Vikram Bakshi (3100 shares) and 48.94 per cent shareholding of Bakshi Holdings (1,42,500 shares). Bakshi Holdings is a separate company with regard to which no order was issued by Recovery Officer. Direction was issued to the Vikram Bakshi by the Recovery Officer with regard to 3100 shares especially and sale proceeds of which shares has already been deposited before the Recovery Officer. [Para 17]

The lifting of veil can be invoked when the corporate entity is in attempt to evade legal obligation or there is necessity to unravel tax evasion. The HUDCO on the strength of Recovery Certificate granted by the Recovery Officer is already taking steps for recovery against the entity. [Para 19]

The order was passed only with regard to 3100 shares held by Vikram Bakshi in CPRPL. The HUDCO has emphasized on the expression 'or any other quantity in the name Vikram Bakshi till further orders' as occurring in the order passed by Recovery Officer. The expression 'or any other quantity in the name of Vikram Bakshi. It is not the case of either of the parties that any more shares apart from 3100 shares are owned by Vikram Bakshi in CPRPL. Hence, the order issued by the Recovery Officer has to be held to be confined to 3100 shares. On the strength of said order, HUDCO is not right in submission that corporate veil of other company in which Vikram Bakshi is also shareholder should also be lifted i.e. Bakshi Holdings. Present is not a case where there is any occasion for lifting corporate veil of other companies which has nothing to do with recovery of Ascot Hotels and Resorts Pvt. Ltd.. HUDCO is fully entitled to recover its dues which are owed by Ascot Hotels and Resorts Pvt. Ltd. On the strength of Recovery Certificate granted by Debts Recovery Tribunal, Recovery Officer in fact is proceedings to effect recovery and certain amount has already been deposited before the Recovery Officer including the value of 3100 shares of Vikram Bakshi, which were under restraint in the Recovery Officer's order. The fact that HUDCO is entitled to pursue its Recovery Certificate cannot be a ground to reject settlement application which has been filed by both the parties. [Para 20]

There are no grounds have been made in intervention application by HUDCO to reject petition for settlement filed by the McDonald's and Vikram Bakshi In result, petition for settlement is allowed and intervention petition is rejected. The impugned order passed by NCLT is set aside. [Para 21]

The assessee was in the business of providing software support/maintenance services and prior to financial year 2015-16 held strategic equity stake of 20 per cent in SAFL. Undisputedly, SAFL was a valuable company having 39 FM broadcasting licenses and FM radio business across various cities in India. SAFL at the material time also held 49 per cent shares in digital broadcasting companies (three in numbers) owning FM radio licenses in metro cities of Delhi, Mumbai and Calcutta. All FM stations were operated under a common and a well known brand named 'Red FM'. The entire share capital of SAFL was held by three entities: the assessee held 20 per cent; Sun TV Ltd. (a listed company) held 60 per cent of the shareholding and South Asia Multimedia Technology Ltd., a Mauritian company held 20 per cent of the equity capital.

■

SAFL required to raise funds for investing in its business and had accordingly offered rights issue at a price of ₹20 per share including share premium of ₹10. The rights issue were fully subscribed and each of the three shareholders subscribed to the rights issue in the ratio of their holding. The assessee subscribed to 2.63 crore shares of SAFL at an aggregate value of ₹20(face value of ₹10 plus premium value of ₹10) aggregating to ₹52.60 crores.

■

A Chartered Accountant (Mr. K.V. Sriram) had determined the FMV of the shares issued by SAFL. In terms of the valuation report dated 17-8-2015, SAFL's net equity value was determined at ₹51.91 crores as per DCF method. The said valuation had not been disputed. It was also not disputed that the Reserve Bank of India [RBI] had also not objected to the subscription of shares by South Asia Multimedia Technologies Ltd. at the price at which the rights shares of SAFL were allotted.

■

The assessee required to raise funds for subscribing to the rights issue offered by SAFL and thus in turn it offered rights issue to its shareholders: Mr. Arjun Rao who held 51 per cent of the assessee's subscribed capital and Max Flexi Services Pvt. Ltd. which held 49 per cent of the assessee's issued and subscribed share capital. For the purpose of determining the FMV, the assessee engaged an expert, J.N. Sharma & Co. (Chartered Accountant). The said expert furnished the valuation report dated 21-9-2015 determining the FMV of the shares of the assessee at ₹2771.65 per share and on the basis of the said valuation the assessee issued a total number of 1,08,976 equity shares to its shareholders at a value of ₹2,772 per share including a share premium of ₹2,762 per share, to its shareholders. The subscription proceeds aggregated ₹30.49 crores.

■

The Assessing Officer did not accept the said valuation as he, inter alia, found that there were certain disclaimers in the valuation report furnished by the Chartered Accountant. The Assessing Officer found that these disclaimers contained in the report rendered the determination of FMV unreliable. The Assessing Officer proceeded to determine the FMV of the shares issued by the assessee at its book value and concluded that the same was in negative. Therefore added a sum of ₹30.38 crores as the assessee's income from other sources under section 56(2)(viib). The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the said decision.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal faulted the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) in calculating the Fair Market Value [FMV] of the shares allotted by the assessee to its existing shareholders by replacing the valuation of equity shares held by the assessee in a downstream company – South Asia FM Ltd. [SAFL]. The assessee had for the purpose of computing the FMV of its shares had valued its holding in SAFL by discounted cash flow [DCF] method; the Assessing Officer had ignored the said valuation and replaced the same by book value of the said investments. Resultantly, the FMV of the shares issued by the assessee to its shareholders significantly reduced.

■

The Tribunal found that the valuation report furnished by the assessee was required to be accepted, as there was no error either in the methodology or the accuracy of the data on which the report was premised. The onus to find fault in the data or the method for calculating the value of the shares as computed in terms of the expert's report furnished by the assessee rested on the Assessing Officer and he had not discharged its onus to do so. The ground on which the Assessing Officer had discredited the expert's report, that is, disclaimers in the report, was rejected and therefore the Tribunal had allowed the assessee's appeal.

On 5-12-1995, US company AT&T and a Birla group company Grasim entered into a Joint Venture Agreement ('JVA'), under which, BCL was to be the Joint Venture Company ('JVC'). Under the joint venture, 51 per cent equity shares of the JVC were to be subscribed and owned by the Birla group and 49 per cent of the equity shares of the JVC were to be subscribed and owned by AT&T-US. Under the JVA, the AT&T-US as a founder was to own and hold 49% equity shares in BCL. Under the JVA, the equity shares subscribed by the founders as party shareholders could be issued in the name of a permitted transferee which was a 100 per cent subsidiary of the founder. AT&T-Mauritius being a 100 per cent subsidiary of AT&T-US was eligible to hold 49 per cent equity shares of JVC as a permitted transferee of the AT&T-US. Accordingly, AT&T-US subscribed to the shares of the JVC and equity shares of the JVC were allotted in the name of AT&T-Mauritius, as a permitted transferee of AT&T-US. Though the equity shares were issued in the name of AT&T-Mauritius under the JVA as a permitted transferee of AT&T-US, all rights in respect of the said equity shares of the JVC like voting rights, rights of management, right of sale or alienation, etc., absolutely vested in AT&T-US.

In October 1997, AT&T-Mauritius and the Birla group executed a document titled as 'confirmation with respect to closing of Joint Venture Agreement'. AT&T-Mauritius was neither a party to the JVA nor was it obliged to pay any amount under the JVA to hold the equity shares of ICL as a permitted transferee of AT&T-US. However, the liability of AT&T-US to pay for the equity shares of the JVC were discharged by AT&T-Mauritius during the period from 1996 to 2003.

Later on Tata group company 'TCL' merged and JVC was restructured. On the other hand, Cingular Wireless of USA acquired shares of AT&T Wireless of USA from AT&T, USA and renamed it as 'NCWS'.

On 26-7-2005, NCWS received an irrevocable offer from an unrelated party, to purchase the shareholdings interest of NCWS in ICL. In terms of the shareholders agreement, NCWS was obliged to offer the shares of ICL first to the other two founders, namely, the Birla Group and the Tata group.

As both the Birla Group and the Tata group were interested in purchasing the entire 74,35,61,480 equity shares of ICL offered by NCWS for US$ 300 million, each Group could get 37,17,80,740 equity shares of ICL on payment of US$ 150 million. Indian Rayon representing the Birla group applied to the DIT International Taxation seeking no objection certificate under section 195 to remit to AT&T-Mauritius the purchase price of equity shares of ICL. The Asstt. DIT, International Taxation, authorized Birla group company namely, Indian Rayon to make payment of US$ 150 million to AT&T-Mauritius without deducting income-tax under section 195(1). Thereupon, Indian Rayon entered into an agreement with AT&T-Mauritius NCWS-US for purchase of equity shares of ICL. Indian Rayon deposited money in the bank account of AT&T-Mauritius and on the same day, the AT&T-Mauritius paid same amount to NCWS-USA.

Accordingly, a Memorandum of Understanding was entered into between WBIDC and the Chatterjee Petrochem (Mauritius) Company CP(M) C and the Tatas on 3-5-1994. In addition to the above, certain duties and obligations to be performed by the Chatterjee Group were also indicated, mainly confined to the question of bringing in equity in an otherwise cash-strapped situation then prevailing in relation to the company's finances. The project started in 1997 and commercial production commenced in August, 2001. Thereafter, further agreements were entered into between the parties and the first of such agreements was entered into on 12-1-2002, whereby CP(M) C, the Government of West Bengal, WBIDC and HPL, inter alia, agreed on a certain course of action in regard to HPL's need of financial and managerial restructuring. WBIDC also agreed to vote along with CP(M) C on all issues in the shareholders meeting and its nominee would also vote along with the nominee directors of the CP(M) C. [Para 99] As dealing with the question whether the payment made on account of termination fees is under an arrangement, understanding or concert etc. with two or more associated enterprises, either or both of which are non-residents, it is essential to bear in mind the fact that termination deed is essentially required to be read with the related framework agreements, which has as its integral part the shareholders agreements and transaction agreements, and share purchase agreement between HTIL and TMT Hinduja, as also HTIL and Indusind Network India Ltd. at its foundation. It is simply not possible to read termination deed in vacuum or to understand termination of option rights in vacuum. How can one interpret deed terminating the framework agreement 2007, unless one looks at framework agreement 2007 itself- which has, at its origin, framework agreement 2006, and none of these framework agreements would have come into existence if the share purchase agreements between TMT Hinduja and Indusind Network and HTIL Mauritius were not to come into existence. When all these documents are put together, the arrangement appears to be like this. HTIL-M, a Mauritius based entity, who had contracted to buy, from two Indian companies by the name of TMT Hinduja and Indusind Network, 54.21 per cent equity capital of ITNL, which in turn, held investments in HEL/VIL, nominates SMMS Investments to buy this equity shareholding, and also arranges for finances to enable such acquisition, by, inter alia arranging guarantee from its ultimate parent company (CGP-Cayman Islands) and by ensuring subscription of, SMMS Investment's equity shares (Rs. 2 crores) and redeemable preference shares by IDFC Investors. However, in order to ensure that SMMS Investors remained in the control of the group entities, the assessee, a group entity, entered into an agreement with IDFC Investors under which assessee had a right to buy entire equity of SMMS Investments from IDFC Investors for a consideration of the same Rs. 2 crores plus interest at the rate of 17.5 per cent per annum - which reflects compensation for the investment of Rs. 2 crores and separately for the allied services rather than the intrinsic worth of the underlying assets of SMMS which are several hundred times more than the agreed consideration. This arrangement was terminated on 24-11-2011, and under the termination arrangement, the shareholdings in SMMS was transferred to TII, another group entity, and yet the assessee, for this loss of opportunity of buying the SMMS equity for a mere Rs. 4.13 crores (i.e. including interest) whereas the said equity was stated to be worth Rs. 1,588.85 crores, pays a further amount of Rs. 21.25 crores to IDFC Investors. The assessee also contends that options were not for a meagre amount as 'a minimum return of 17.5 per cent was stipulated- this does not qualify as a meagre amount'. However, it is this plea of the assessee which infact demonstrates that the IDFC Investors, who was under an option to sell entire equity of SMMS at an agreed price of 2 crores plus 17.5 per cent interest, was nothing more than a financial investor- something much less than a genuine investor as the connotation of this expression are known in the commercial world. [Para 100]

Flow of attribution of profits in Judicial Context : The Observed Transition

Evolution of attribution of profits in judicial context

Anglo French Textile Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 101 (SC) is one of the early rulings in Indian Judiciary on attribution dating to the year 1952. The Supreme Court ('SC') considered figure of 10% on British Indian sales as reasonable for attribution, basis the extent of operations carried out in British India. Similarly, in Hukum Chand Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1967] 63 ITR 232 (SC), based facts of the case, 15% allocation was considered reasonable for operations relating to contracts undertaken in British India (in the pre-independence era the territory of British India was demarcated from Indore, where the company had operational mills for manufacturing textiles.) In arriving at this figure, emphasis was laid on the then Rule 33 of the Income Tax Rules, 1922. Rule 33 has now been replicated as Rule 10 explained above.

In recent past, rulings pertaining to profit attribution were pronounced considering Rule 10 together with specific provisions in the Act. In Dy. DIT (International Taxation) v. Nipro Asia Pte Ltd. [2017] 79 taxmann.com 154 (Delhi - Trib.)6, the AO, in absence of any correct TP study, adopted provisions of Rule 10 using 'selective financial figures' from public websites. ITAT rejected AO's computation (negating use of publicly available data) and assessed income based on Section 44BB and 44BBB of the Act which provides for presumptive profit rate of 10%. Similar view was upheld in Nortel Networks India International Inc. v. Dy. CIT (International Taxation) [2014] 65 SOT 158 (URO)/49 taxmann.com 147 (Delhi - Trib.) and GE Energy Parts Inc. v. ADIT (International Taxation) [2017] 78 taxmann.com 2 (Delhi - Trib.)

Going further, in Motorola Inc., ITAT allocated 20% profits to PE contending that PE played role in negotiation and conclusion of contracts and supply of equipment in India. Similarly, in Galileo International Inc., 15% profit attribution was considered sufficient owing to the role played by PE in negotiating contracts.

Formulary Apportionment in attribution of profits

In 2013, in Convergys Customer Management Group Inc. v Asstt. DIT [2013] 58 SOT 69/34 taxmann.com 24 (Delhi - Trib.), formulary apportionment was adopted as the basis of allocation. The Tribunal used end customer revenue as the base to which a global operating income percentage was applied to arrive at profits attributable to the Indian operations.

In India, current provisions on attribution as defined under Rule 10 are akin to the formulary approach. However, globally, there has been no agreement on the use of formulary apportionment owing to practical difficulties.

Importance of FAR analysis in Arms-Length attribution of profits

Landmark decision by SC in DIT (International Taxation) v. Morgan Stanley and Co. [2007] 292 ITR 416/162 Taxman 165 (SC) Inc. throws light on the importance of transfer pricing analysis in attribution of profits to PE. It lays, "The impugned ruling is correct in principle insofar as the associated enterprise, that also constitutes a PE, has been remunerated on an arm's length basis taking into account all the risk-taking functions of the enterprise. In such cases, nothing further would be left to be attributed to the PE."

Similarly, in Rolls Royce Singapore (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. DIT [2012] 347 ITR 192/202 Taxman 45/13 taxmann.com 81 (Delhi), it was emphasized that profits attributable to PE in India is made having regard to FAR Analysis. The AO held that 25% of the profits on sale of spare parts to customers in India was chargeable to tax which was reduced to 10% by CIT (A)7 and upheld by ITAT. To substantiate this reduction, it explained, "The risk assumed by PE in India is very limited. It is only performing the functions of soliciting contracts for sale of assessee's products or promoting the sales. All other main or core activities regarding the arrangements or acquisition of products supplied by the assessee company to the Indian customers are performed in Singapore."Hence, a detailed transfer pricing analysis is imperative.

In a recent decision in Arrow Electronics India Limited, a Singapore Company, opened Liaison Office ('LO') in Bangalore which was established to be the Indian PE. Placing considerable reliance on FAR analysis for profit attribution, it was held, "there is no mathematical formula for working out profits of Indian operations and that of Singapore operations. Functions, Assets and Risk analysis is the best way to arrive at profits". Allocation of weights in terms of functions performed, risk borne and assets owned (FAR) by the LO formed basis of profit allocation. The final quantification computed by AO, based on detailed FAR analysis, upheld by the Tribunal, was attributable as 40:60 to the LO and the Head Office.

It is well settled that the scope of interference with the finding given by the Single Judge in appeal filed under Letters Patent is limited and the Court, as an appellate Court, is not expected to substitute its own view to the view taken by the Single Judge and if the Court comes to the conclusion that the finding given by the Single Judge is not perverse or contrary to the law, it should not interfere with the said order. [Para 45]

The finding given by the Single Judge that BIIL and BIL is a part of a single entity is neither perverse nor illegal. The findings given by the Single Judge are concurred with and there is no reason to interfere with the order passed by the Single Judge. [Para 46]

Therefore no case is made out for interfering with the judgment and order passed by the Single Judge. Appeal is, therefore, dismissed. [Para 47]

HELD: There is no dispute as to the nature of Compulsorily Convertible Debentures. A debenture indisputably creates and recognizes the existence of a debt and till it is discharged, either by payment or by conversion, the debenture would essentially represent a debt. A Compulsorily Convertible Debenture is a debt which is compulsorily liable to be discharged by conversion into equity. Any amount payable by the issuer of debentures to its holder would usually be interest in the hands of the holder.

According to Stroud's Judicial Dictionary of Words and Phrases (5th Edition), interest means, inter alia, compensation paid by the borrower to the lender for deprivation of the use of his money. Concededly, gains arising from sale of capital assets would not be in the nature of interest. The expression 'interest' as defined under section 2(28A) cannot apply to all gains that are received by a debenture holder (lender) irrespective of the transaction resulting in such gains. As an illustration, a lender may assign its debt to a third party and if such debt is held as a capital asset, the gain or loss arising from the transaction would be a capital gain/loss in the hands of a lender and would not be construed as interest.

ISSUE OF APPLICABILITY OF ADVANCE RULINGS The American company 'M' filed an application before the Authority for Advance Ruling seeking a ruling in respect of the stock option scheme framed by it. As per the scheme framed by 'M', an option was given to employees of the Indian subsidiary company 'MI' to avail the shares of 'M'. Under the scheme, the employees of 'MI' wouldhave the option to subscribe to the shares of 'M' at a pre-determined price which was otherwise known as 'option price', which would be lower than the market price of the shares. The employees had the option to subscribe and become owner of the shares on the date of their choice. As and when such option would be exercised, the employees would have to sell the shares in the open market in the USA at the ruling stock market price. The net gain would be paid to the employees of 'MI' in India. The Authority for Advance Ruling, found that the taxability of the amount gained by exercising the option was not in doubt. The Authority further observed that it was a perquisite or profit arising out of the employment. Therefore, the Authority concluded that the profit arising out of exercising of the stock option should be treated as 'salary'. The contention of 'M' of the USA before the Authority for Advance Ruling was that the Stock Option Scheme was formulated by the American company and not by the Indian company and, therefore, it could not be a perquisite or salary paid by the employer. While adjudicating this issue, the Authority for Advance Ruling found that the Indian Company was a fully owned subsidiary of the American company and the business of the Indian company was completely controlled by the parent company in America. The object of making such offer to the employees was only with a desire to give benefit to the employees and at the same time enhancing their interest in the company. The Authority for Advance Ruling further found that the parent company made such an offer to the employees of the subsidiary company only because it regarded its subsidiary and itself as the same concern. It was further found that even if the subsidiary was treated as a separate juristic entity, the stock option offered by the American company must be treated to have been made for and on behalf of the Indian company. Ultimately, it was concluded that the scheme devised by the American company was to give encouragement and pecuniary incentive to the employees of the Indian company by offering the employees the option to purchase its shares at a pre-determined price. This sort of option would not be possible unless the parent company treated its own business and the business of the Indian subsidiary company as one. Accordingly, the Authority for Advance Ruling found that the gain made by the employees after exercising the stock option would be taxable as salary in India. It was not in dispute that the assessee was granted stock option on the basis of the scheme framed by 'M', which was the subject-matter of the proceeding before the Authority for Advance Ruling. This decision of the Authority for Advance Ruling was pronounced on 18-11-1998. Therefore, it was not correct to say that the Indian subsidiary company 'MI' was incorporated in India only in the year 1999 and the stock option was granted even before the incorporation of the Indian subsidiary company. The very fact that 'M', moved an application before the Authority for Advance Ruling and the decision was rendered on 18-11-1998 in respect of the very same Stock Option Scheme said to be promoted by the 'M' showed that the Indian subsidiary company was in existence even before that. Moreover, the decision of the Authority for Advance Ruling is binding. [Para 10]

In view of section 245S(1)(b ), the decision of the Authority for Advance Ruling in respect of the Stock Option Scheme was binding on the assessee also. Therefore, whatever is said by the Authority for Advance Ruling in respect of the Stock Option Scheme promoted by 'M' of the USA, is binding on the assessee and the Indian subsidiary company. Therefore, the profit arising out of the exercising of stock option by the assessee was only a salary within the meaning of section 15. [Para11]

ISSUE OF ACCRUAL OR ARISING OF INCOME IN OR OUTSIDE INDIA

The CBDT had considered the issue regarding taxability of the perquisite on shares issued to the employees at less than market price and issued instructions in Circular No. 710, dated 24-7-1995. Clause 2(iii ) of the circular clearly says that where the employer has offered its shares to its employees at a price lower than the one at which the shares have been offered to the other shareholders/public, the difference between the two prices would be taxed as perquisite. Therefore, the difference between the price offered by 'M' and the ruling market price was liable to be taxed. [Para 12]

a branch qualifies as a Permanent Establishment ("PE") of its head office. Accordingly, the business profits, to the extent attributable to that branch, become taxable in host country. Further, a branch may also be taxed in India since a branch is considered an extension of the head office and not a separate legal entity. This would amount to double taxation of the branch profits. That said, one does get double tax relief by way of tax credits in the home country of residence, against taxes paid overseas. The possible guard against such PE, leading to taxation exposure of the Indian company overseas, is setting up an independent subsidiary company in the host country. A company is treated as a separate legal entity for legal and tax purposes. Unlike branch, a company is ordinarily treated as a resident of the country in which it is incorporated. On the flip side, the compliance burden of a company is usually more than that of other forms of presence. Further, dividend declared by the subsidiary may be subject to withholding tax or distribution tax. The proposed Controlled Foreign Company ("CFC") provisions, as part of the Direct Tax Code, could expose the profits of the subsidiary to tax in India even if no income is actually distributed/declared by the foreign subsidiary, in certain passive income situations. Other anti-avoidance measures like Transfer Pricing ("TP") regulations and the proposed General Anti-Avoidance Rule ("GAAR") provisions also add to the complexities.

MODE OF OUTBOUND INVESTMENT

An Indian company desiring to establish its presence overseas is permitted to set up a company or participate in a joint venture overseas, subject to the existing FEMA regulations. Under FEMA, the Indian party can make overseas investments upto 400 pe rcent of its net worth as on the date of the last audited balance sheet. Further, any financial commitment above USD 1 billion or its equivalent in a financial year will require prior permission from the RBI, even if the financial commitment is within the prescribed limit. The overseas investment helps the Indian company in achieving various objectives such as access to newer markets, expanding distribution network, raw material sourcing, global scale of operation, inorganic growth, proximity to global customer, managing/spreading risk, fund raising etc.

The simplest mode of making an ODI is to establish a subsidiary in the host country (direct method). As regards the taxability of foreign sourced income, it is relevant to note that an Indian company is taxable on its global income under the Income-tax Act, 1961 ("Act"). Accordingly, the income repatriated by the overseas subsidiary by way of dividends would be taxable in India at a concessional rate of 15 per cent.

Another interesting and prevalent mode of making an ODI is by interposing an Intermediate Holding Company ("IHC") in a tax efficient jurisdiction (indirect method). A structure involving IHC could potentially result in favourable tax treatment since the Indian company may be better positioned in terms of tax efficient deployment of profits as well as exit. However, setting up of IHC in a tax efficient jurisdiction without any commercial substance and with the primary objective of obtaining a tax benefit is open to challenge by the tax authorities, both in India and in the eventual jurisdiction where business is undertaken via such IHC.

USE OF OFFSHORE FINANCIAL CENTERS

Large business houses structure the cross border investments by channelizing them through Offshore Financial Centers ("OFC"). An OFC, though not precisely defined is usually a small, low-tax jurisdiction specializing in providing corporate and commercial services to non-resident offshore companies, and for the investment of offshore funds.

Though it is alleged that corporations use OFCs primarily to minimize taxes and banking privacy afforded by the OFCs (which is rapidly falling away due to exchange of information), there are a number of genuine purposes for which OFCs could be and are used by corporations. To name a few:

(i)

Effective movement of capital and resources;

(ii)

Provide legal protection to intangibles;

(iii)

Enable their purpose as an intermediary holding company;

(iv)

Reduction in costs by providing centralized group services or shared services; and

(v)

Low tax jurisdictions which help corporations save significant taxes and reduce the impact of transfer pricing rules in home countries.

Choosing an OFC is dependent on various tax and non-tax factors like tax rates, withholding rates, tax incentives, anti-avoidance rules, treaty network, commercial and legal infrastructure, political and economic stability, accessibility to capital markets, flexibility afforded under local corporate laws, and availability of skilled human capital.

Some of the commonly used OFCs, with which India has inked DTAAs, are Cyprus, Ireland, Luxembourg, Mauritius, Netherlands, Switzerland, Singapore and Malta. Such DTAAs go beyond Tax Information Exchange Agreements, that do not go to afford protection or relief from double taxation.

Further, most OFCs offer participation exemption to the holding company. Participation exemption typically provides that certain types of dividends are not taxed in the hands of qualifying shareholders. In addition, many participation exemption regimes provide that capital gains on shares are not taxed as long as a specified proportion of the company's share capital is held for a specified period.

The assessee-company was incorporated on 3-4-2008. The Assessing Officer sought details and information under section 133(6) from the subscribers to the share capital and share premium account. On a perusal of the above findings, as recorded by the Assessing Officer, it will be evidently clear that the entire controversy involved in the matter is fully factual.

The submission that the assessee did not have adequate opportunity to put forth their case is not agreeable, as the Assessing Officer has recorded that the assessee has been represented by the authorized representative and if according to the assessee, the documents have not been properly appreciated or to be appreciated in the manner as decided by the assessee, it is for the assessee to agitate the same before the appellate authority and there is no justifiable or valid reason for the assessee to bypass the appellate remedy available under the Act.

The fact is that the writ petition was of the year 2011 and was pending before this Court all these years. The Assessing Officer has gone on record to state that the Dubai company, which was stated to be a Government company, is no longer a Government company on account of the change in the shareholder pattern. To dislodge these findings, the assessee has to necessarily bring in facts and documents to establish their stand and this cannot be permitted to be done in a writ petition.

The return pertains to investments by way of direct or portfolio investments, reinvested earnings and other capital investments in the Indian company made from 1st April to 31st March of the previous year.

Non Compliance/Violation of Pricing Guidelines

Pricing Guidelines, as discussed above, plays a pivotal role for any company who plans to secure foreign investment, thus it would not be far-fetched to convey the importance of their compliances. Point 3 of Annexure 6 of the Consolidated FDI Policy 2017 provides for the violation of any provision under the regulations, shall be taken up for investigation of such contravention by the Directorate of Enforcement under the Ministry of Finance. The erstwhile FEMA 20R under Paragraph 5 of Schedule I provided that one should apply for compounding proceedings in case of violation of pricing guidelines for issue of shares. In cases, where transfer of capital instruments from resident to non-residents, at a price which falls outside the pricing guidelines specified by the Reserve Bank from time to time, prior approval of the RBI is required.

Delhi High Court in their ruling in Tata Docomo case wherein one of the many issues that arose, the HC pondered whether RBI's approval was required, i.e. RBI could in fact regulate an arbitral award (in the nature of damages) to be remitted if such transfer was in violation of pricing guidelines under FEMA?

The HC rejected the RBI's plea on various grounds starting with questioning their locus in the case while observing that the arbitral award entitled NTT Docomo to exercise its right under the shareholders agreement to have its shares under the joint venture bought by Tata Sons at a price which was equal to 50% of its original investment. The enforcement of the award was objected to by Tata Sons and RBI on the ground that enforcement of the award would constitute a violation of FEMA and related regulations since the shares were to be sold/purchased at a predetermined rate.

The court held that since the award was in the nature of damages, no FEMA provision had been violated. Further, given the nature of the award, no special permission of the RBI was needed for the remittance either.

Delhi High Court in April 2016 in case Virtuous Retail Ltd. v. Kakade Construction Co. (P.)[O.M.P. 399 of 2013, dated 29-4-2016] observed:

With a view to complying with the provisions of the FEMA, the respondents, Kakade Construction Company Pvt & Ors., commissioned valuation reports from Jones Lang and LaSalle and MZSK & Associates, whose valuation reports indicated that the shares held by the Petitioner, Virtuous Retail Limited, in KCMPL, are valued at a maximum of approximately Rs. 43.9 crore and Rs. 35 crore, respectively. India is increasingly being recognized as a global player with significant cross-border investments. During a time when emerging market economies are under transition, a number of Indian private players, are increasingly expanding their footprints in foreign lands through direct investments with a view to achieve regional and global reach. Companies are seeking more imaginative ways to optimize their internal cash management, often resorting to related party transactions. Due to several business and commercial factors, Indian companies have opened branches or subsidiaries outside India.

TRENDS

Overseas direct investments by Indian companies more than doubled to USD 5.23 billion in March 2014 as compared to USD 2.16 billion in March 2013, according to data released by the Reserve Bank of India ("RBI"). Other investments in the form of equities, loans and guarantees were USD 2.91 billion, USD 418.72 million and USD 1.91 billion, respectively, during the period.

With Indian corporations increasingly looking at expanding their global footprint by investing overseas, the Netherlands and Singapore have attracted most of the outward foreign direct investments from India, with a share of 28.8 per cent and 15.2 per cent respectively in total investments.

In the next 15 years, more than 2,200 Indian firms are anticipated to invest in markets overseas. The integration of the country's economy with the rest of the world has given the domestic corporate sector access to global networks and markets, transfer of technologies and skills and has also facilitated research and development ("R&D") for value addition. The Government of India's supportive policy regime, coupled with India Inc's experimental orientation, is certain to demonstrate an upward trend in Overseas Direct Investment ("ODI") in the years to come. Indian outbound investment finds its way into established and developed markets such as the US, BRICS economies such as Brazil and Russia, the next wave of emerging economies such as Indonesia, Eastern Europe and Middle East and lucrative markets such as the African continent.

This article highlights illustrative considerations involved in outbound investment by Indian companies.

ACCELERATING GROWTH

There are several strategic factors that have motivated Indian Industries to become active in global markets and focus on making cross-border acquisitions to achieve the next level of growth. One of the factors motivating Indian corporations is to look for assets abroad to enter into new markets. It is not easy for a new firm to break into developed markets because those markets are already mature and the various relative competitive disadvantages, (such as high start-up cost, establishing distribution channels and dealer networks from scratch, creating brand awareness etc.) create barriers to entry.

The other factor for domestic companies is product and technology access, which is limited in a greenfield environment. To leapfrog over the issue of building from scratch, companies may acquire a target with product diversity and ability to provide sustainable brand or technology advantage.

Additionally, the companies in developing countries realized that they need to be vertically integrated in order to improve procurement and drive margin growth. This trend has been especially seen in case of natural resources wherein companies have acquired mines in natural resource-intensive markets in order to obtain low-cost coal supplies to generate power offshore; so also with acquisition of offshore oil blocks.

NATURE OF ENTITY TO BE SET-UP

While business considerations are a crucial factor in the selection of a particular type of entity, one also needs to consider tax implications which largely depend on the form of entity chosen. Where the primary focus of an enterprise is gauging or exploring a foreign market, a liaison office may be considered. However, in case of multifaceted operations, a branch or a subsidiary are better forms of doing business. A branch has restricted business scope due to constraints around investment and activity. With growing levels of investment and function, a transition to a subsidiary structure is fait accompli.

Generally, under the domestic tax laws of the host country, a branch creates a "business connection" of the company in the host country and accordingly its profits are taxable in the host country at rates applicable. Even under the Double Tax Avoidance Agreements ("DTAAs"), a branch qualifies as a Permanent Establishment ("PE") of its head office. Accordingly, the business profits, to the extent attributable to that branch, become taxable in host country. Further, a branch may also be taxed in India since a branch is considered an extension of the head office and not a separate legal entity. This would amount to double taxation of the branch profits. That said, one does get double tax relief by way of tax credits in the home country of residence, against taxes paid overseas.

13. Common Interpretational Issues and the Practitioner’s View

13.1 Net worth: standalone or consolidated?

Rule 2(1)(p) imports section 2(57) of the Companies Act, 2013, which is a standalone concept. An Indian holding company with significant subsidiary value embedded in its books cannot inflate its net worth on a consolidated basis to expand its 400% ceiling. Where group capacity is needed, the group company guarantee route under Regulation 5(1)(ii), with each guarantor’s independent ceiling, is the structurally correct path.

13.2 Group company guarantees and netting of fund-based exposure

The first proviso to Regulation 5(2) requires that where a group company extends a guarantee, any fund-based exposure it has to or from the Indian entity is deducted from its net worth in computing its own ceiling. This is the OI Regulations’ anti-double-counting rule, but it is also a planning trap, because a routine inter-company loan can shrink the guarantor’s available headroom. Periodic review of inter-company balances is therefore not just a tax-transfer-pricing exercise but an FEMA capacity exercise.

13.3 The promoter group concept

The second proviso to Regulation 5(2) requires that where the guarantee is extended by a body corporate or individual promoter, the Indian entity must be part of the promoter’s ‘promoter group’ as defined in the SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018. Practitioners structuring family-business outbound investments should confirm the promoter-group mapping with reference to the SEBI ICDR Regulation 2(1)(pp) definition rather than relying on a colloquial understanding of ‘group’.

13.4 Investment in a holding-company foreign entity

Rule 9(1) expressly recognises that an Indian entity may invest in a foreign entity engaged in bona fide business activity “directly or through step down subsidiary or the special-purpose vehicle”. This puts to rest the older debate on whether a pure holding-company structure abroad qualifies as ‘bona fide business’ - it does, provided the structure as a whole is engaged in bona fide business and the two-layer cap under Rule 19(3) is observed (where the foreign entity also invests into India).

What is tax evasion, tax avoidance and when the corporate veil can be lifted has been elucidated by the Supreme Court in the case of Vodafone International Holdings B.V. (supra). It was held that, in the context of taxation of holding structures, the initial burden lies on the Revenue to allege and establish abuse in the nature of tax avoidance in the creation or use of such structures.In the application of a judicial anti-avoidance rule, the revenue may invoke the 'substance over form' principle or 'piercing the corporate veil' test only after it is able to establish on the basis of the facts and circumstances surrounding the transaction that the impugned transaction is a sham or tax avoidant. If a structure is used for circular trading or round tripping or to pay bribes then such transactions, though having a legal form, should be discarded by applying the test of fiscal nullity. Similarly, where in a holding structure an entity which has no commercial/business substance has been interposed only to avoid tax, it would be open to the Revenue to discard such inter-positioning, but this has to be done at the threshold. A legal right is an enforceable right. The question is what is the nature of the 'control' that a parent company has over its subsidiary. But barring such cases, the legal position of any company incorporated abroad is that its powers, functions and responsibilities are governed by the law of its incorporation. No multinational company can operate in a foreign jurisdiction save by operating independently as a 'good local citizen'. Lifting the corporate veil doctrine is readily applied in tax cases. M&A Impact Assessment: Case Studies Indian corporate sector is witnessing a sudden spurt in M&A activities since 1991. Further, it has been established that Indian corporate sector is witnessing the first ever merger wave since 1996-97 (Kar, 2005). Therefore, it becomes all the more important to know the success of M&As. The success of M&A could be ascertained on the basis of financial performance of the corporate enterprises. This chapter aims at evaluating the importance of M&A on corporate performance through case studies. Further, an attempt is made to find out the nature, pattern add motivations of M&As. Micro level analysis of selected companies has been carried out to investigate the impact of M&As on the basis of financial variables identified from research literature.

Research Findings

Summary of the research literature on impact of M&As mainly points towards two sets of hypotheses. First, M&A has been favourable to the corporates through increased performance. The researchers contributing to this line of arguments include, Baldwin & Gorecki (1987), Lithchenberg (1992), Hughes (1993) Switzer (1996) and Vander (1996). The other set of authors who found that M&A has not led to increase in performance include Newbound (1970), Kitching (1974), Singh (1974), Utton (1974), Meeks (1977), Ravenscraft & Scherer (1987 and 1989), Caves (1989), Tarasafsky & Covari (1991) and Tsakalotos (1997).

Literature on Indian M&As is very few. Some of these studies have made an attempt to study the impact of M&As on profitability of the merged companies. Das (2000) compares the pre merger and post merger operating profit margin for a sample of 14 acquiring firms and find a decline in profitability in 8 of these companies after merger. The study of Saple (2000) supports these findings. It observes that mergers did not lead to an improvement in performance as measured by profitability (return over net assets) adjusted for the industry average. Beena (1998) also finds no significant difference in the/rate of return and profit margin between the periods before and after the mergers. In case of acquiring companies, it has been observed that M&As found to be beneficial as companies grew in size and profitability (Kar, 2005).(ii)

Impact on Performance

The impact of M&As on Indian corporate enterprises has been stated in the following company based case narratives. This analysis has been designed to present a comparative picture of pre M&A and post M&A performance for the sampled companies. Secondly, an attempt has been made to find out the strategic motives which drive these companies to go for M&As and try to investigate its impact on the growth of studied companies.

1. Ranbaxy Laboratories Limited

Background: Incorporated in June 1961 as a private limited company, Ranbaxy Laboratories (RLL) manufactures and markets pharmaceutical dosage forms (for human health care), animal health care products, bulk drugs and intermediates, diagnostics, laboratory chemicals and reagents. It is the largest exporter of bulk drugs and pharmaceutical dosage forms in India. RLL has three successful overseas joint ventures in Nigeria, Malaysia and Thailand. The bulk antibiotics plant at Toansa, Punjab, has been approved by the US FDA and the dosage forms pharmaceuticals plant at Dewas, MP, is accredited by the World Health Organization (WHO). The plants for bulk cephalosporin at Mohali and bulk fluoroquinolones at Dewas have also been designed to conform to FDA standards. It went public in October 1993 to part-finance manufacturing facilities of bulk fluoroquinolones at Dewas, MP; and dosage forms at Poanta Sahib, Himachal Pradesh. In 1996 it acquired six leading brands from Gufic. Croslands Research Laboratories; a leading manufacturer of dermatological pharmaceutical formulations has been merged with RLL. In 1997-98, it entered into a 50:50 joint venture with the New Jersey-based Schein Pharmaceuticals Inc., the generics arm of Bayer AG, Germany, for manufacture of Ranitidine. The company is the first to launch prescription products under its own label in the United States. On 28th December, 1998, the company issued bonus shares in the ratio of one new equity share for every one equity share held. In March 2000, it launched Clarinifast, a novel drug compound that belongs to the VLA (Very Large Antigen) a class of drug which represents a totally new mechanism for treatment of asthma. No such drug has been launched in the international market.

The express language of Section 56(2)(viib) states "any consideration for issue of shares".

In Asstt. CIT v. Golden Line Studio (P.) Ltd.6, the Tribunal held that preference shares stand on a totally different footing as compared to equity shares and thus section 56(2)(viib) cannot be made to apply circumstances.

In the case of conversion (CCDs), the capital has already been contributed by way of debentures earlier and is now merely changing from 'loan' to 'equity'. In other words, there is no fresh infusion of funds in case of conversion and therefore there is no logic in applying the strict deeming provision of 56(2)(viib) which is an anti-abuse provision.

Since Section 56(2)(viib) is a deeming provision, it needs to be construed strictly. In order to prevent any arbitrary or ad-hoc exercise of power, the legislature did not leave it open to tax authorities to bring within its purview any transaction except 'issue of shares' as expressly stipulated in the section. Therefore, CCDs and Preference shares should remain outside the scope of Section 56(2)(viib).

PLANNING AROUND ANGEL TAX

DPIIT Registration - According to an official from the Revenue Department, Over 80,000 DPIIT-registered start-ups will not come within the angel tax purview. Hence, DPIIT registration is the first and foremost way around angel tax. However, this is only applicable to entities meeting thresholds of having a paid-up capital of not more than INR 25 crores and revenue of not more than INR 100 crores. For entities unable to meet DPIIT thresholds, the following may be pertinent:

Choice of Entity and Jurisdiction

Flip Structure – Setting up companies outside India and raising money there, instead of in India

If money is to be raised in India, then raise funds through notified entities in specified territories. Full or part investment may be through Notified entity combined with Price Matching Method, but within the 90-day period, and this FMV can be relied upon for resident investors as well.

Choice of Instrument

Instead of going for the traditional choice of instrument (equity), start-ups might move towards debt instruments for raising funds from foreign investors.

CCPS – Technically not shares but there is still a risk of challenge from the tax department at the lower levels.

CCDs – There are much stronger judicial precedents7 that debentures cannot be equated with shares, and hence, this might prove to be a safer option for raising funds.

Tightening Valuations

Start-ups looking to go ahead with foreign investments while disregarding the risk of challenges from the tax department must look into the following safeguards for their valuations:

1.

Maintain Robust Valuation Report

2.

Backup projections based on underlying facts,

3.

Using growth rates/ metrics that can be defended,

4.

Realistic assumptions on revenue & costs,

5.

Sanity check on Valuation Report Disclaimers,

6.

Legal jurisprudence on valuation is fairly established in favor of the taxpayer on the ground that valuation by an expert cannot be challenged.8

CONCLUSION

The premise of angel tax was supposedly restricting the influx of 'black money' through capital markets. However, the same logic does not seem to be applied by tax authorities since 2012, as evinced by the continued strain of litigation on start-ups receiving funding through proper banking channels. With funds such as Sequoia and Blackstone having billions of dollars at their behest, does one really need a provision to confirm the creditworthiness and source of funds?

Section 56(2)(viib) might be outlasting its stated objective when Indian entrepreneurs are having to consider shifting HQs abroad. The Finance Ministry may need to rethink the new provisions, as the start-up industry which was hoping for a breather after the Covid shock, received a jolt themselves.

(iii)

Since right from the outset the FMO was aware that the FDI policy and the statutory FEMA Regulations permit FDI in townships, construction of houses, only by way of equity investments and the FDI policy and the FEMA Regulations prohibits any other form of investments (non-equity) in the said sector with an assured return/rate of return and, therefore, structured the above device to bypass/circumvent/nullify the FDI policy and the FEMA Regulations, the Plaintiff which is admittedly acting at the instance of FMO cannot be heard to say that FMO was induced by the Defendant to make the FOI/Investment through incorrect representations/assurances. The FMO is as much a party to the aforestated colourable device/structure designed as the Defendant Company. The case law relied upon by the Plaintiff, therefore, does not lend any assistance to the Plaintiff.

(iv)

The Plaintiff is acting at the instance of FMO/FMO nominees on the Board of Directors of Vinca and are by the present Suit, seeking the assistance of the Court, to enforce and recover the FDI amount and interest thereon at 14.5 per cent per annum for FMO (through Vinca), contrary to the prohibition contained in the FDI policy and FEMA Regulations. This as the Supreme Court has held is clearly and patently inconsistent with the paramount consideration of public interest. [Para 26]

It is contended on behalf of the Plaintiff that Vinca has a township project at Village Kanjur which is an FDI eligible project under Press Note 2 of 2005 and that accordingly the FDI investment in Vinca was in accordance with Press Note 2 of 2005. [Para 27]

From the aforestated facts it is clear that Vinca was interposed as the holding company of Amazia and Rubix only for the purposes of the said transaction/FDI by FMO and Vinca was only the nominal recipient of the FDI. The SSA and the annexed DTDS made it clear that Vinca was not entitled to retain the FDI amount, or to utilize the same in any of its own projects. The SSA and DTD required Vinca to immediately pass on the FDI amount received from FMO to Amazia and Rubix against subscription of OPCDs issued or to be issued by them (i.e. Amazia and Rubix). Press Note 2 of 2005 permits FDI investment in the real estate sector only if it is for a township/construction project. Accordingly the purported 'investment in Vinca' cannot be said to be in accordance with Press Note 2 of 2005 and was not FDI/FEMA complaint. [Para 27.1]

It has been further contended on behalf of the Plaintiff that Vinca is a separate legal entity and that it was open for Vinca to invest its funds in Amazia and Rubix. Once the FDI investment was made by FMO in Vinca, the funds belonged to Vinca and there was no prohibition against Vinca investing the said amount received by it from FMO, in OPCDs of Amazia and Rubix and the investment by Vinca could not be treated as an investment by FMO. [Para 28]

The above submission advanced on behalf of the Plaintiff also cannot be accepted. The SSA and DTD establish that there was no question of Vinca deciding of its own volition to invest the FDI amount received by it from FMO in the OPCDs of Amazia and Rubix. The specific/express terms of the SSA and DTD stipulated that Vinca could not retain, or itself utilize the FDI amounts received by it from FMO, but was required to immediately pass on the same to Amazia and Rubix against subscription of the OPCDs issued/to be issued by them. Accordingly, there was no question of Vinca choosing to invest in Amazia and Rubix or of Vinca investing 'its funds' in the OPCDs of Amazia and Rubix. The investment of the FDI amounts by FMO in OPCDs of Amazia and Rubix through Vinca, was contractually pre-ordained/pre-determined. [Para 28.1]
